## Abhidhamma Piṭaka
## Vibhaṅgamūlaṭīkā
## Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Khandhavibhaṅga
## 1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā
"Catusaccadaso" means: the Four Truths brought together by the mind are called "Catusacca"; because He has seen these Four Truths, He is called "Catusaccadaso" (Seer of the Four Truths). Although disciples (sāvakas) and Paccekabuddhas also possess the vision of the Four Truths, the Buddha's vision of the Four Truths is not preceded by another's [teaching]. Furthermore, because He attained Omniscience (sabbaññutā-ñāṇa) regarding those Four Truths, and attained mastery (vasībhāva) over the Ten Powers (dasabala) [or the truths of effect], and because [His vision] is very clear as it is spread throughout the mental continuities of others, it should be understood that the Buddha alone especially deserves the praise "Catusaccadaso."

He is called "Nātha" because of the derivation "nāthati." He desires the welfare and happiness of those to be disciplined (veneyyas). Alternatively, He burns away the destruction caused by defilements within the mental continuities of others. Or, it means He requests such and such beneficial practice, in the manner of: "Monks, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on his own accomplishments such as virtue," and so forth. He is called "Nātha" because He is the Supreme Lord (Paramissara) who is endowed with supreme mastery over the mind, or who masters and overcomes all beings through His qualities such as virtue.

Having stated the reason why this commentary is worthy of being heard—"I shall compose it having paid respect to the True Dhamma"—and wishing to urge [the listeners] once more to listen, he said: "Listen to that [commentary] with a concentrated mind." Alternatively, having stated the reason for listening respectfully with the words "I shall compose it having delved into the method of the ancient commentaries," and wishing to urge them to that respectful listening, he said: "Listen to that [commentary] having paid respect to the True Dhamma."
2:
In this context, the phrase "Seer of the Four Truths" (Catusaccadaso) should be understood as praise based on the quality of having a number equal to the Dhammasaṅgaṇī teaching, which has four divisions. The phrase "endowed with the eighteen Buddha-dhamma" is also praise based on the qualities having a number equal to the Vibhaṅga teaching, which has eighteen divisions.

In another way, because the Buddha saw the Four Truths in an unsurpassed manner as mentioned above, He was able to teach the Dhammasaṅgaṇī in four ways. Because He was endowed with the eighteen Buddha-dhamma, He was able to teach the Vibhaṅga in eighteen ways. The words "Seer of the Four Truths, endowed with the eighteen Buddha-dhamma" indicate the qualities that enable the teaching of such discourses. By showing this, it clarifies that these teachings are unerringly true because they were spoken by the Omniscient Buddha, thereby urging beings to learn and practice these teachings. By showing his own effort in completing the work, [the author] also inspires respect in listening to the commentary. By showing that those who are not omniscient and lack the aforementioned qualities are unable to teach the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and Vibhaṅga, he generates exceptional respect for these texts and their commentaries. Furthermore, he clarifies the qualities of the Triple Gem, such as the Buddha's state of being a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha).

Among those qualities, the Four Truths are already well-known. The eighteen Buddha-dhamma, however, should be understood as follows: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, has unobstructed knowledge regarding the past. He has unobstructed knowledge regarding the future. He has unobstructed knowledge regarding the present. Of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these three qualities, all bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and follow knowledge. All verbal actions are preceded by knowledge and follow knowledge. All mental actions are preceded by knowledge and follow knowledge. Of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these six qualities, there is no loss of zeal (chanda), no loss of teaching the Dhamma (dhamma-desanā), no loss of energy (vīriya), no loss of concentration (samādhi), no loss of wisdom (paññā), and no loss of liberation (vimutti). Of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these twelve qualities, there is no playfulness (davā), no hasty speech (ravā), no unperceived [by knowledge] (afuṭa), no hurriedness (vegāyitatta), no unheeding mind (abyāvaṭamano), and no unreflecting equanimity (appaṭisaṅkhānupekkhā)."

Among those qualities, "no playfulness" means there is no action with the intent of playing. "No hasty speech" means there is no sudden [unintentional] action. "No unperceived [by knowledge]" means there is nothing not touched or known by His knowledge. "No hurriedness" means there is no rushed action. "No unheeding mind" means there is no occurrence of useless thought. "No unreflecting equanimity" means there is no equanimity devoid of knowledge. In some versions, however, instead of "no loss of teaching the Dhamma," they write "no loss of zeal, no loss of energy, no loss of power (satti)."

In the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, after grouping the states such as wholesome (kusala) by way of triads (tika) and dyads (duka), the Vibhaṅga was taught to analyze those same states according to the Suttanta method by way of aggregates (khandha) and so on.
3:
In this text, the detailed analysis of the aggregates and so forth, which were taught in brief, is called Vibhaṅga. The specific Pali text in which these various analyses are mostly treated and understood is called "Vibhaṅgappakaraṇa" (The Book of Analysis). "Adhikato" means that which is taken specifically as being worthy of being taught.

In the Khandhavibhaṅga, which is the beginning of that Vibhaṅgappakaraṇa, the passage "The five aggregates are the aggregate of form... the aggregate of consciousness" is called the Suttantabhājanīya (Suttanta Analysis). If one asks, "Is only this much of the text the Suttantabhājanīya?", the answer is: Yes, however, by the word "iti," which indicates the meaning of "beginning" or "variety," all of the Suttantabhājanīya is included. Thus, this passage starting with "the aggregate of consciousness" or "having varieties such as the aggregate of consciousness" should be understood as the Suttantabhājanīya. Alternatively, it is a demonstration of the whole by a part, like someone pointing out a mountain or an ocean. In that Vibhaṅgappakaraṇa, the Khandhavibhaṅga is taught at the beginning because the aggregates encompass all phenomena except Nibbāna, and because they have fewer terms than the āyatanas and so forth, which also encompass everything.

"Not less than those five" means that because form and so forth do not have the nature of feeling and so forth, and because in that nature (such as wholesome states) where past and other states are to be spoken of as a heap, there is no other nature besides these five natures like ruppana (deformation). This is said with reference to the fact that among numbers lower than five, conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata dhammas) would remain unfinished and incomplete. It is not said with reference to the mere absence of numbers below five. Because there is no sixth aggregate, it is said "not more than that." This is because Nibbāna, which is a single entity, free from the varieties of past and so forth, and devoid of the state of being past and so forth, does not have the meaning of a "heap" (rāsi).

By the word "Rāsimhi," the scope of the word "khandha" is shown along with the meaning of "heap." By the words "guṇe paṇṇattiyaṃ ruḷhiyaṃ," only the scope of the word "khandha" is shown, not the etymological meaning of the word. The word "khandha," occurring when taking without remainder the qualities such as virtue (sīla) which have mundane and supramundane divisions, indicates the meaning of a heap distinguished by qualities like virtue. However, some teachers say, "In this context, the meaning of quality (guṇa) is the meaning of aggregate (khandha)." In the case of "dārukhandha" (a log of wood), the word "khandha" does not occur in the sense of the word "paññatti" (designation); rather, because the designation "dārukhandha" occurs for such a broad and long piece of wood, it is said to fall under "paññatti." Similarly, the word "khandha" in "viññāṇakkhandha" occurring in a single consciousness does not state the meaning of the word "ruḷhi" (usage); however, when the word "khandha," which is well-known for a collection, occurs for a part of that collection, it occurs by that very usage (ruḷhi). Thus, it is said that the word "khandha" falls under "ruḷhi."

It should be understood that the use of the ablative case (nissakkavacana) in all instances such as "rāsito guṇato" is intended to show that the scope itself is the cause for the occurrence of the word "khandha." This meaning of "rāsito"...
4:
In order to show the definition by the power of the meaning of the word as well, it is said: "This meaning of 'khandha' is the meaning of 'a heap' (piṇḍa)," and so forth. If the meaning of "khandha" were the meaning of "portion" (koṭṭhāsa), there would have to be a sixth aggregate. For Nibbāna is also a sixth portion. Therefore, it is appropriate to say, "The meaning of 'khandha' is the meaning of 'a heap' (rāsi)." Alternatively, for those phenomena that have divisions by way of past and so forth, their state as various portions is stated by the power of their respective characteristics such as deformation (ruppana). Thus, it should be understood that Nibbāna, being free from divisions like past and so forth, is not taught as an aggregate either by the meaning of "portion" or by the meaning of "heap."

By the phrase "this much," only the summary (uddesa) is intended. "The four great elements... form"—thus it is analyzed. Where is it analyzed? It occurs in eleven instances (okāsa). By the word "iti," which indicates an illustration, all methods of analysis are shown. This analysis, as well as the analysis of the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so forth in instances such as the gross (oḷārika), should be applied to the eleven instances as appropriate. The same applies to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and so forth. As for the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), it is analyzed specifically as the six groups of consciousness, "eye-consciousness... mind-consciousness," in the first five of the eleven instances. In those instances, there is no analysis as mind-element (manodhātu) or mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu). To show that those two are intended by "mind-consciousness," it should be noted that the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) says "mind-element, mind-consciousness-element."

Having thus shown the definition of phenomena in the five aggregates according to the method of the Pali text, it is said "api ca" (moreover) and so forth to show it again by another method. "Here" (ettha) means in this Exposition of the Aggregates (Khandhaniddesa).

## 1. Description of the Exposition of the Aggregate of Form (Rūpakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā)

In the phrase "yaṃ kiñci" (whatever), the word "yaṃ" is an indefinite indication in a general sense, and the word "kiñci" is an indefinite indication that touches upon other types and divisions. By both words, everything that is worthy of being indicated in the neuter gender is encompassed and included: whether past... or near, whether small or great, of whatever kind or such a kind. Therefore, seeing that it might also apply to other meanings worthy of being indicated in the neuter gender besides form, "rūpaṃ" (form) is said to restrict the over-application that arises by exceeding the intended meaning. Taking the word "yaṃ" and the word "kiṃ" together with the particle "yaṃ kiñci" as a single term because they indicate a single indefinite meaning, it is said "padadvayena" (by two words).

"Monks, what [kind of phenomenon] do you call form?" means: You also call form "form"; for what reason do you call it so? Alternatively, it means: For what reason is it called form? Speak of that reason.
5:
The meaning is 'Speak the reason.' Then, when those monks remained silent, the Blessed One said, 'It is called form (rūpa) because it is affected (ruppati),' and so forth.

'It is broken' (bhijjati) is said with reference to the breaking of the previous continuity of matter, because when opposing factors such as cold and so forth meet, a subsequent continuity of matter that is dissimilar to the previous one is seen to arise. Since breaking (bheda) is simply the arrival at a transformation that is dissimilar to the previous matter, 'it is broken' (bhijjati) means it undergoes transformation. Undergoing transformation is the arising of new matter that is dissimilar to the previous matter upon encountering cold and so forth. As for the mental aggregates, because they change very rapidly, there is no meeting with other factors in the same way that material phenomena meet with cold and so forth during their moment of presence (ṭhitikkhaṇa). Just as causes such as temperature (utu) or nutriment (āhāra) that have reached the moment of presence cannot produce a material continuity similar to the previous one due to such a meeting, in the same way, there is no meeting with other causes in the case of mental phenomena. The term 'ruppana' (being affected) is well-known in the sense of undergoing transformation due to impact; therefore, because mental phenomena are free from impact and because they do not have a distinct transformation like material phenomena, they are not called 'ruppanti' (they are affected) or 'ruppanalakkhaṇā' (having the characteristic of being affected). It should be understood that transformation due to hunger and thirst also occurs because of the meeting with the internal fire (udaraggi).

Here, by the word 'kuppati' (it is disturbed), the derivation of the word 'rūpa' in the active sense (kattu) is shown; by the words 'ghaṭṭīyati' (it is struck) and 'pīḷīyati' (it is oppressed), it is shown in the passive sense (kamma). This is because the action of transformation and so forth is itself the action of 'ruppana'. Because that meaning, which is both active and passive, is subject to breaking, it is said 'the meaning is: it is broken' (bhijjati) to show this sense. Alternatively, the derivation of the word 'rūpa' is stated in the middle sense (kammakattu) as 'it is rūpa because it is affected' (ruppatīti rūpaṃ). For transformation itself is called 'ruppana'. For that very reason, the meaning is shown by the word 'bhijjati' in the middle sense as 'the meaning is: it is broken'. Whatever matter undergoes transformation and is broken, the meaning of the term has been made clear by these words because of its being disturbed, struck, and oppressed. In accordance with the question 'In what sense?' (kenaṭṭhena), it is said 'In the sense of being affected' (ruppanaṭṭhena). Since 'ruppana' is not only the literal meaning of the word but also the characteristic of that meaning, it is said by virtue of the characteristic of the meaning: 'It is also appropriate to call it rūpa because of the characteristic of being affected'.

'Having been cut' (chijjitvā) means having been severed, either because of falling [from a mountain foot] after becoming faint, or because the wind cuts the major and minor limbs. In the phrase 'with extremely caustic cold water' (accantakhārena sītodakena), the term 'extremely caustic' (accantakhāra) might be said with reference to the state of being extremely cold. That water, which is the cause for the world's duration, which brings about fulfillment, and which supports the earth, should not be caustic like the water that destroys the world. For if it were so caustic, the earth would dissolve. 'In the Avīci Great Hell' refers to the Avīci Hell together with its surrounding subsidiary hells (ussada). For that very reason, it is said 'For there...' and so forth. 'Petti... they are not' means that there are indeed beings of such a nature; it is because there is no fixed rule that they must only be of such a nature. The same applies to the Kālakañjika Asuras and others. By the words 'they go crawling' (sarantā gacchanti), the meaning of the word 'sarīsapa' (reptile) is stated.
6:
## In the word 'abhisaññūhitvā', there is also the meaning 'having made a collection'.
In this word 'abhisaññūhitvā', there is also the meaning 'having made a collection'. Thus, by this statement 'all matter... is shown', it demonstrates the nature of the term 'rūpakkhandha' as a descriptive compound with a common referent (samānādhikaraṇa-kammadhāraya-samāsa). For that very reason, [the author of the Saṅgaha] says, 'Apart from matter... there is none.'

## In the word 'pakkhipitvā', it means 'having included matter in the eleven categories'.
In this word 'pakkhipitvā', it means having included matter in the eleven categories. In those eleven instances, it is not that only the matrix (mātikā) is included and established; rather, it is the matter relevant to the context that is included and established as the matrix.

## By the alternative method... 'it is included in this very count', it shows that 'atītaṃsena' is an instrumental case used in the sense of the locative.
Alternatively, by the statement 'it is included in this very count', it shows that the term 'atītaṃsena' is a word with an instrumental case ending used in the sense of the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti). To show the distinction of the great essentials (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) by which it is counted, the Buddha said, 'The four great essentials,' and so on. In this sense, it implies that the distinction of great essentials and derived matter is the reason for the counting in the past portion.

This statement is not for the purpose of excluding states such as feeling (vedanā) belonging to the past portion, because those states like feeling have already been excluded by the phrase 'yaṃ rūpaṃ' (whatever matter). Nor is it for the purpose of excluding other distinctions of matter, because all distinctions have already been counted in that past portion. Nor is it for the purpose of excluding the future and present modes, because those have already been excluded by the term 'atītaṃsa' (past portion).

Otherwise, if the intended meaning is that matter counted in the past portion is counted as 'the four great essentials... matter', then this statement would merely show another method of counting, not the distinction of states counted in the past portion. Even in showing that other method of counting, the meaning that it is counted in the past portion by way of the distinction of primary matter and derived matter still follows, because that is its nature. Such a distinction of primary matter and derived matter should not be the reason for counting in the past portion, because matter of such nature is also counted in the present and future, and states with the nature of pleasure (sukha), etc., are also counted in the past portion. Therefore, only the former method is appropriate. In the internal description (ajjhatta-niddesa) and external description (bahiddha-niddesa) as well, only the kind of meaning mentioned in that former method is obtained.

## The phrase 'suttantapariyāyato' is said because the Sutta is a figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā).
The phrase 'suttantapariyāyato' is said because the Sutta is a figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā).

## The phrase 'abhidhammaniddesato' is said because the Abhidhamma is an abstract teaching (nippariyāya-desanā), and 'niddesa' is defined as a teaching by way of definitive determination.
The phrase 'abhidhammaniddesato' is said because the Abhidhamma is an abstract teaching (nippariyāya-desanā), and 'niddesa' is defined as a teaching by way of definitive determination.

In the Pali passages beginning with 'kiñcāpi', this is the intended meaning: Since it is a Suttanta classification (Suttanta-bhājanīya), just as in Suttas such as 'One should not follow the past', the state of being past, etc., is taught only by way of duration (addhāna), so too should it be indicated here. Nevertheless, even the Suttanta classification is indeed an Abhidhamma teaching, because it proceeds by way of selecting and analyzing the states taught in the Suttas through detailed classification; thus, the state of being past, etc., is indicated only by way of the Abhidhamma description.
7:
In this phrase 'by way of duration (addhā), continuity (santati), occasion (samaya), and moment (khaṇa)', it is understood through Suttas such as 'Did I exist in the past duration?' that the word 'addhā' applies to the time delimited by death (cuti) and rebirth (paṭisandhi). However, in this Pali passage, 'Monks, there are these three durations. Which three? The past duration, the future duration, and the present duration,' the duration delimited in the ultimate sense (paramattha) is appropriately delimited by the moment (khaṇa) according to the Niruttipatha Sutta. For in that Sutta, the Buddha taught the present state of existing matter, saying, 'Monks, whatever matter has been born, has appeared, that is called "it exists" (atthi),' as well as the past and future states before and after that. Generally, however, since the past and other durations delimited by death and rebirth are taught in the Suttas, that very duration is mentioned here as 'by way of duration (addhā)'.

Cold is of the same kind (sabhāga) as cold; likewise, heat is of the same kind as heat. Whatever cold or heat, having fallen upon the body and proceeding by way of continuity, is uniform without deficiency or excess, that temperature is called 'one temperature' (eka-utu). Because the similar temperature (sabhāga-utu) is of an indefinite nature, the designation 'one' is made; the same applies to nutriment (āhāra). 'Arising from one cognitive process (vīthi) and one impulsion (javana)' is stated by way of the five doors and the sixth, the mind-door. The explanation of continuity (santati) and occasion (samaya) is stated in the Commentaries for the benefit of those practicing insight (vipassanā).

Matter whose functions of the productive cause (janaka-hetu) and the supportive cause (upatthambhaka-paccaya) have been completed is called past matter. Matter whose function of the productive cause has been completed but whose function of the supportive cause has not yet been completed is called present matter. Matter that has not yet reached both functions is called future matter. Matter that exists at the moment of performing its own function is called present matter. The cause that produces is called 'hetu'; the cause that supports is called 'paccaya'; the producing and supporting by those causes is called 'function' (kicca). Just as a seed produces a sprout and the earth, etc., support that sprout; and just as kamma produces kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) and its result (vipāka), and nutriment, etc., support those material and mental states; in this way, the functions of the productive causes such as kamma-condition (kamma-paccaya) and proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya), and the functions of the supportive causes such as co-nascence (sahajāta), pre-nascence (purejāta), and post-nascence (pacchājāta) conditions for each material group (rūpa-kalāpa) and mental arising (cittuppāda) should be applied as applicable. Therein, the function of the productive cause (hetu-kicca) should be noted at the moment of arising (uppāda-khaṇa), and the function of the supportive cause (paccaya-kicca) should be noted at all three moments. The specific functions of earth, etc., such as supporting, and the specific functions of contact (phassa), etc., such as touching, are called 'one's own function' (sakicca); the moment of performing that function is called 'the moment of one's own function' (sakicca-khaṇa). Alternatively, it is called 'sakicca' because it occurs together with its function; the moment in which matter or mind occurs together with its own function is 'the moment of one's own function', and the state existing at that moment is called 'present'.

'Ettakam-eva' (only this much) refers only to the meaning stated by the repetitive phrase 'tesaṃ tesaṃ' which has the sense of pervasion. Showing 'of another, of another' is called 'apara-dīpana' (further clarification).
8:
By this phrase “should seek” (pariyesatūti), it is shown that the act of seeking is not a reason for the removal (or prohibition) of the designation “undesirable” (aniṭṭha). Indeed, due to the fault of karma or the fault of perversion of mind (citta-vippallāsa), creatures such as dung-eating worms and the like, as well as madmen and the like, might seek [such things]. Furthermore, due to perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vippallāsa), those such as the Yonakas might also seek [them]. It is not because the object has a nature worthy of being sought that they seek it; rather, it is because it has a nature not worthy of being sought that this object is named “undesirable” (aniṭṭha). This is the meaning.

“Due to the absence of attainment” (sampatti-virahato) means due to the absence of attainment (sampatti)—which is the state of being a result of wholesome karma and being prosperous and beautiful—within the successful celestial and human realms of visible forms and so on. Because of such absence of attainment, that undesirable object should not be sought. Certain beautiful forms, such as those of elephants and the like, arise due to unwholesome karma and thus do not become a cause of happiness for those creatures like elephants. To encompass such forms, the term “unpleasant” (akanta) is used. The reason is that for various beings, only the form produced by their own wholesome karma becomes a cause of happiness, while that produced by unwholesome karma becomes a cause of suffering. Therefore, the state of being desirable (iṭṭha) or undesirable (aniṭṭha) of karma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) should be applied only in relation to the being who performed the karma.

In the Commentary, however, it is only stated that “there is no undesirable matter born of wholesome karma”; it is not stated that “there is no desirable matter born of unwholesome karma.” By not stating this, it would seem to allow that a beautiful form, even if born of unwholesome karma, could be a desirable object (iṭṭha-rūpa) for other beings. Teachers say that matter born of wholesome karma is indeed desirable for everyone, both oneself and others.

For certain animals, the human form is unpleasant; therefore, they flee as soon as they see a human. Humans, too, are frightened when they see the form of a deity. Although they flee in fear, their resultant eye-consciousness (vipāka-cakkhuviññāṇa) arises as a wholesome resultant (kusala-vipāka) in reference to that form. However, some teachers suggest that because they lack the merit to appreciate such an object, they find no delight in it. Just as there is no undesirable matter born of wholesome karma, it should also be said that there is no beautiful, desirable matter born of unwholesome karma. This is because the matter born of the unwholesome karma of creatures like elephants is only an object of unwholesome resultant (akusala-vipāka) for humans. Only matter born of wholesome karma arising during the course of existence (pavatti) is the object of wholesome resultant. However, it can be said that because it is mixed with desirable objects, a small amount of matter born of unwholesome karma will not be the cause for the frequent arising of unwholesome resultants. Since the resultant consciousness (vipāka-viññāṇa) cannot be deceived regarding any object, the classification of desirable and undesirable objects by way of resultant is very sound. Therefore, following the power of that resultant, the state of being desirable or undesirable should be applied to all objects.

## Why is it said, “The five cords of sensual pleasure are undesirable” (aniṭṭhā pañca kāmaguṇā)? Is it not taught in passages such as “Visible forms cognizable by the eye are desirable” that visible forms and so on, which are only desirable, are “cords of sensual pleasure” (kāmaguṇa)?
9:
Because they can be called “sensual cords” in a sense similar to [actual] sensual cords; and this similarity lies merely in being visible forms and so on, not in being desirable (iṭṭha). Or, by the word “undesirable” (aniṭṭha), the state of not being a sensual cord is shown; thus, visible forms and so on that are dissimilar to desirable sensual cords are called “sensual cords,” just as an inauspicious statue is called “Siva” (Auspicious). Alternatively, all visible forms and so on, whether desirable or undesirable, are indeed sensual cords because they are the grounds for craving (taṇhā). Has it not been taught: “Visible forms in the world are of a dear nature, of a pleasant nature,” and so on? However, because they are exceedingly desirable (kāmanīya), the Suttas refer to desirable visible forms and so on as “cords of sensual pleasure” (kāmaguṇa).

In both terms “inferior” (hīna) and “superior” (paṇīta), the mention of “being born of unwholesome karma” and “being born of wholesome karma” should be understood as a classification made by fixing upon the beings, as in “of those various beings.” Since karma-born matter is distinct among the matter included within the continuity of a being, it is said to be “by way of karma-born matter.” If the genitive case in “of those various beings” is used to denote the relationship between the object and the possessor, then it should be understood that the classification is not made by karma-born matter alone, but by the power of all matter born of the four causes (catuja-rūpa) connected with the faculties (indriya). Here, since the method is shown through the evident visible forms and so on, the state of being inferior or superior should also be applied to the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) and so on.

“Culminating in the pleasing” (manāpapariyanta) means: “Among the five cords of sensual pleasure, I declare the pleasing object to be the ultimate limit.” What is the reason? Because those objects are pleasing to some and unpleasing to others. To whomever they are pleasing, for that person, they are the supreme. Therefore, the supremacy of the sensual cords occurs by the power of the inclination (ajjhāsaya) of each individual, not by the inherent nature of the objects themselves.

By the method taught in this Sutta, because of the occurrence of both enjoyment and anger toward the same object, and because the inherent nature of an object does not possess the state of being desirable or undesirable, and because the undesirable is taken as “desirable” and the desirable is taken as “undesirable,” it means there is no separately classified desirable or undesirable as such. Except for Nibbāna, the grasping of objects as desirable or undesirable occurs in other objects due to the perversion of perception (saññā-vippallāsa). It is like the perception of bitterness in milk, sugar, and the like by those who are mad or whose bile is disordered, arising through the power of perverted perception. Aiming at this meaning, it is shown that they “culminate in the pleasing” (manāpapariyanta).
10:
"Vibhattaṃ" means having the sense of being distinguished. Alternatively, it means having the sense of being analyzed in detail and shown by the teachers of the Commentaries. Those pleasant (iṭṭha) and unpleasant (aniṭṭha) objects are also distinguished and shown by way of the average being (majjhimaka-satta). For other individuals, by way of perversion (vipallāsa), it means this object is pleasant or unpleasant. In taking the unpleasant as pleasant and the pleasant as unpleasant among these undistortedly distinguished pleasant and unpleasant objects, the perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa) is not the only cause; it can also be said that there is the state of being a cause for the arising of wholesome resultant (kusala-vipāka) and unwholesome resultant (akusala-vipāka) due to the disturbance of elements (dhātu-kkhobha) and the alteration of the sense faculties (indriya-vikāra), etc.

Indeed, cold water is a cause for the body-consciousness (kāya-viññāṇa) which is a wholesome resultant for those oppressed by the heat of the sun, but it is a cause for an unwholesome resultant for those oppressed by cold. The touch of cotton is a cause of suffering (an unpleasant object) on a wound, but a cause of happiness (a pleasant object) for one without a wound. Massaging with a young hand produces happiness, but striking with that same hand produces suffering. Therefore, it is appropriate to distinguish the object by way of the resultant (vipāka).

By the words beginning with "Kiñcāpi," it is shown that although there is perversion of perception, only wholesome resultant arises in such things as seeing the form of the Buddha, and only unwholesome resultant arises in such things as seeing excrement; thus, the pleasantness or unpleasantness of the object is shown by that resultant. Showing the fixity of the resultant by the object even when perversion of perception exists is done only for the purpose of indicating the fixity of the object.

Furthermore, by the words beginning with "Api ca dvāravasena," it should be understood that the pleasantness or unpleasantness is shown by way of the resultant, because an object which is a cause of suffering or happiness in one door can produce a resultant of happiness or suffering in another door, and because in the very same door, a similar tangible object such as a gem can produce happiness or suffering through gentle touching or hard striking.

"Heṭṭhima-naya" (the lower method) is the method taught beginning with "despised by those various beings" (Vibhaṅga, 6), taking the object distinguished by way of the average being and the resultant. "Sammuti-manāpa" is the pleasing form conventionally determined and distinguished by way of the average being and the resultant. That form is already distinguished by its nature and should not be broken, so the meaning is that He does not break it. However, "puggala-manāpa," which is taken as pleasing by individuals such as hell-beings through perversion of perception, is broken by the subsequent method beginning with "Taṃ taṃ vā pana." The form of the Vemānika-petas is also said to be "inferior to the human form" because it arises from unwholesome kamma and is a basis for suffering such as torture.
11:
Gross matter (oḷārika-rūpa) should be understood as being easily grasped by knowledge through the impact of the base and the object, whereas subtle matter (sukhuma-rūpa) is difficult to grasp by knowledge because of the absence of such impact. Due to the very sense of being difficult to grasp by knowledge, the state of being difficult to penetrate the characteristics should be noted. The word "dasavidhaṃ" (tenfold) is spoken to show the gross matter that is not directly called "distant" (dūre). However, even the matter called (subtle matter) can indeed be distant (dūra) in terms of location.

The method described below (heṭṭhima-naya) is the method concluded by showing "femininity faculty... etc... this is called matter in the vicinity (santike)" by way of characteristics and by way of location distinguished by the measure of twelve cubits. That method, because it concludes by taking distant and near matter together by way of characteristic and location, proceeds by making a mixture while dividing (the distant and near). Alternatively, "bhindamāno" (dividing) means it proceeds by separating characteristic and location, such as by characteristic through showing the own-nature and by location through the word yevāpanaka. Alternatively, it is said "bhindamāno gato" (proceeded while dividing) because it proceeds by making the near and distant by characteristic into distant and near by location, thereby breaking the state of being near to make it distant, and breaking the state of being distant to make it near.

In this context, however, in this Pali text "Taṃ taṃ vā pana rūpaṃ upādāya upādāya," the Blessed One does not break the distant matter by characteristic by making it near by location according to the previous method, nor by separating it from matter distant by location, nor by mixing it with matter distant by location. If so, what does He do? He breaks only the matter that is distant by location. In this context, the meaning should not be taken in three ways according to the method previously mentioned. This is because He does not make matter that is distant by location into matter that is near by characteristic, nor does He separate it by characteristic or mix it with that (near matter) by characteristic. Only the making of matter that is distant by location into matter that is near by location is to be understood here as "breaking (bhedana)."

In this context, in the phrase "does not break distant matter by characteristic," it does not mean that He does not perform the breaking by the three methods mentioned previously. Rather, because the state of being distant or near does not exist based on the very characteristic of matter that is near or distant by characteristic, the not making of matter that is distant by characteristic into matter that is near by characteristic is to be understood as the not breaking of matter that is distant by characteristic. This shows only this much: that this method is not like the previous method. In that passage "bhindamāno," breaking (bhedana) was spoken of in one way, and in this context, breaking is spoken of in another way.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Aggregate of Matter is finished.
12:
## 2. Explanation of the Description of the Aggregate of Feeling (Vedanākkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā)

Sensitive matter (pasāda rūpa) such as the eye and so forth are included in the gross sense-sphere selfhood (kāmāvacara attabhāva) as well as in the mind-made selfhood (manomaya attabhāva) produced by jhāna. Therefore, neutral feelings (adukkhamasukha vedanā) which have those sensitive matters as their physical basis are figuratively called 'bodily' (kāyika). They are not called 'bodily' because they have the body-sensitivity (kāyapasāda) as their physical basis. This is because sensitive matters such as the eye and so forth are not the body-sensitivity.

In this context of "by way of continuity (santati) or by way of moment (khana)," the state of being past and so forth is not mentioned by way of duration (addhā) and time (samaya) because of the distinction between various feelings such as pleasure (sukha) and so forth. A single pleasant feeling itself cannot be past, future, and present within a single duration or time. Likewise, painful feelings and neutral feelings differ as being bodily, mental, and so forth. Therefore, only the collection of feelings (vedanāsamudaya) deserves to be called past and so forth by way of duration and time. This is because the collection of feelings can be delimited by those durations and times. However, since only parts of feelings are taken here, they deserve to be delimited only by continuity and moment.

Even within a single continuity (santati), various feelings such as pleasure and so forth can exist. When taking a specific distinction among those feelings that deserves to be delimited, there should be a continuity that can delimit that distinct feeling—one that is manifest, occurring in the doors and objects associated with that feeling, and occurring in uninterrupted association with the single kind of object that produces it. Therefore, continuity is taken as the delimiting factor without considering other specific feelings. Alternatively, because states that change rapidly deserve to be delimited only by their change, the delimitation is stated by way of continuity and moment. By the words "those that have gone to the preceding end, the following end, and the middle," the method already stated by way of root-cause (hetu) and condition (paccaya) is shown.

Because of association with the fire of defilements (kilesa), they occur with distress (sadaratha). By this statement, grossness (oḷārika) is shown by way of nature. By the words "dukkhavipākaṭṭhena," grossness is shown by way of the function of producing gross results (vipāka). Resultant feelings (vipāka vedanā) lack effort (nirussāha) because they are cast by the force of kamma and are bound to kamma, and because they are devoid of activities (byāpāra) such as bodily kamma. Functional feelings (kiriya vedanā), although possessing effort (sa-ussāha), have no result. Wholesome and unwholesome states that have results are gross, like a pregnant woman. Therefore, their opposites, the resultless (indeterminate) feelings, are called subtle (sukhuma).

"Asātaṭṭhena" means by way of the sense of being unpleasant. By that word, the undesirable nature (aniṭṭha), which is the opposite of the pleasant, is shown. "Dukkhaṭṭhena" means by way of the sense of being painfully felt. By that word, the burning function of painful feelings is shown. According to the words, "Venerable Sir, that which is neutral feeling (adukkhamasukha vedanā), the Blessed One has spoken of it as being included in peaceful and sublime pleasure," neutral feeling is very peaceful because it lacks the nature of spreading (pharaṇa) and because it is not the domain of the underlying tendencies (anusaya) of sensual lust and aversion, which are not peaceful. It is called sublime (paṇīta) because it reaches a prominent state, being attainable by exhausting the attachment to pleasure. Likewise, it should be understood that equanimity (upekkhā), which has a similar distinction such as being associated with knowledge or dissociated from knowledge within the same class, without mixing with the sense-sphere class and so forth, is more sublime than pleasant feeling.
13:
Neutral feeling is peaceful because it is devoid of the nature of spreading and because it is not the repeated locus of the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion, which are not peaceful. It is called sublime (paṇīta) because it reaches a prominent state, being attainable by exhausting the attachment to pleasure. Likewise, equanimity (upekkhā) attained without exhausting the attachment to pleasure should also be applied as being more sublime than pleasure of the same class, such as those associated with knowledge or dissociated from knowledge, without mixing with the sense-sphere class and so forth.

Because it is the condition for the elements (dhātu) that have increased, pleasant feeling causes agitation; because it is the condition for the elements that are oppressed, painful feeling also causes agitation. Both pleasure and pain are said to "pervade" (pharati) because they arise as if spreading through the body. "Madayamānaṃ" means causing intoxication. "Chādayamānaṃ" means producing desire or overwhelming. Just as the body of one oppressed by the heat of the sun becomes refreshed and increased when sprinkled with a jar of cool water, so too is the body of one endowed with pleasure; thus it is said "as if being sprinkled."

"Ekattanimitteyeva" means occurring only in an object of a single nature, such as the earth kasina. "Carati" means it is subtle because it lacks the vibration found in sense-sphere impulsions (javana) that have various advertings (āvajjana).

One is "unskilled" (akovida) because of lack of skill in the Blessed One's intention. As it appears in the Wholesome Triad (Kusalattika) and so forth, it should be known that "wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross; indeterminate (avyākata) feelings are subtle." The passage beginning with "yampi" is started to show the distinction between the levels of planes (bhūmi). By this method, one who speaks of grossness and subtlety in those very planes by way of the distinction of nature, such as "sense-sphere equanimity is subtler than sense-sphere pleasure," does not destroy the method.

Mundane and supramundane are taught in combination. Therefore, just as the inferior and sublime are extracted in the purely sublime supramundane, so too should the inferior and sublime be extracted as far as possible in the purely inferior unwholesome. The meaning is that there should be no hesitation in such extraction, as it is already permitted.

Some say that because unwholesome states are not subtler than wholesome ones and because the Pali text is unchangeable, "the lower method should not be looked at." However, even when speaking by way of this or that alternative (vāpana), there is no change; thus it is not said with reference to change. It should be understood that because the lower method has already been stated, it is proper to take the unstated method and say "or rather this or that" (taṃ taṃ vā pana); thus it is said "the lower method should not be looked at." Unwholesome states with many results are gross due to the abundance of hatred (dosa/kilesa); wholesome states with few results are similar. Unwholesome states with few results are subtle due to the weakness of hatred; wholesome states with many results are similar. Because they are the basis for attachment to the gross and the subtle, the sense-sphere and so forth...
14:
There are states of being gross (oḷārika) and subtle (sukhuma). By the word "sāpi," it should be understood that just as the wholesome feeling consisting in meditation (bhāvanāmaya) is shown by way of division, the method of showing the respective divisions of feelings consisting in giving (dānamaya) and virtue (sīlamaya) is also shown. Alternatively, in the phrase "sāpi," it should be applied by taking the meaning as "all three kinds" (tividhāpi).

Having dissimilar groups by virtue of class (jāti) and so forth is called dissimilarity (visabhāgaṭṭha). Having dissimilar functions or dissimilar natures by virtue of having painful results and so forth is called distinctness (visaṃsaṭṭha); it does not mean non-association (asampayoga). If it were so (non-association), then by being the opposite of "far" (dūra), it would become "near" (santika). In that case, due to the state of being mixed, it would arrive at the state of being near. In reality, one feeling has no association (sampayoga) with another feeling. Also, in the explanation of the term "near" (santika), it will be said, "by way of being of the same class (sabhāga) and by way of being similar (sarikkha)." Therefore, the meaning should be understood only in the manner already stated.

Why is it said, "The near should not be extracted from the far"? Just as the far unwholesome (rooted in hate) is extracted and shown as "far" (dūra) from the near unwholesome (rooted in greed), is it not possible to extract and show another wholesome state as "near" (santika) from that far wholesome state? It is not possible. For if that were so, by considering that a wholesome state is near to another wholesome state, it would amount to extracting only the near from the near. In that case, it would only result in expressions like "nearer than the near." Here, being far or near is spoken of only by way of comparison. Therefore, just as it is impossible to extract the far from the far, it is also impossible to extract the near from the near. This is because "farther than the far" and "nearer than the near" are not intended.

If it were said, "Although a wholesome state is not extracted as being near to another wholesome state, it is far from a certain unwholesome state and near to that [other] unwholesome state," that is not so. For a wholesome state is never near to an unwholesome state. Again, if it were said, "A certain unwholesome state is near to a wholesome state, and that unwholesome state should be extracted from the far wholesome state," that also is not so. Since there is no unwholesome state in the wholesome, there is nothing to be extracted as being near to it. Therefore, because the "far" (dūra) taught here is extremely dissimilar (visabhāga), there is no near in the far, and thus the near cannot be extracted from the far. However, if the "near" taught here is divided, the far can be found within that very [near] category; hence it is said, "The far should be extracted from the near."

Even by way of comparison, the near cannot be extracted from the far. If it is said that the feeling associated with hate (dosasahagata) is far from the feeling associated with greed (lobhasahagata), and the feeling associated with greed is near, it amounts to extracting the near only from the near. Likewise, it is the same when saying that the feeling associated with greed is far from the feeling associated with hate, and the feeling associated with hate is near.
15:
In this Exposition of the Aggregate of Feeling as well, because one similar (sabhāga) feeling is extracted from another similar feeling, one is not able to say, "The feeling associated with hate is far from the feeling associated with greed, and that very [feeling associated with greed] is near." This is because there is no cause for the feeling associated with hate to be in a state of nearness (with greed). Therefore, because the state of dissimilarity (visabhāga) does not occur without taking distinction, the near cannot be extracted from the far by way of farness (dūratā) which does not pervade all similar states. Indeed, the feeling associated with hate does not occur pervading the entire unwholesome class. However, because the state of similarity (sabhāgatā) occurs by including distinction within it, the far can be extracted from the near by way of nearness (santikatā) which can pervade all dissimilar states. This is because the state of being unwholesome pervades all dissimilar states such as those associated with greed and so forth. Therefore, it is said, "The near should not be extracted from the far," and so on.

## The Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Feeling is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Perception

In the passage "perception born of eye-contact" (cakkhusamphassajā saññā), although the name of contact (phassa) is derived from the basis (vatthu, i.e., the eye-basis) and the name of perception (saññā) is derived from contact, the perception distinguished by the contact which is distinguished by the basis is also distinguished by the basis. Like contact, that perception also has that [eye] basis as its support; therefore, it is called "a name derived from the basis." In the passage "perception born of impingement-contact" (paṭighasamphassajā saññā) as well, just as contact arises due to the impingement of the basis and the object, so too the perception born from that contact is called "a name derived from the basis and the object." Here, it should be understood that "impingement-contact" (paṭighasamphassa) is said by dropping the latter term, meaning contact born of impingement, or contact to be known by impingement.

The mental aggregates (nāma-khandha) which occur depending on names in the state of being known, or which are governed by names, or which have designation (adhivacana) as their manifestation, are called "designations" (adhivacana). Contact born of those mental aggregates is "designation-contact" (adhivacanasamphassa). Or, contact itself is both designation and contact for the reasons already stated, thus it is "designation-contact." Or, contact to be known by designation is "designation-contact." Perception born from or in that designation-contact is "born of designation-contact" (adhivacanasamphassajā). Since the aforementioned meaning is also possible in contact occurring at the five doors, by that figurative method (pariyāya), the perception born therefrom is also called "born of designation-contact." However, just as perception born of mind-contact (manosamphassajā) is called "born of designation-contact" in the primary sense (nippariyāyena) because no other variety (such as impingement-contact) is possible, this perception born of impingement-contact is not so called [in the primary sense] because another distinct variety (impingement-contact) is possible—this is the intended meaning.
16: If this is so, since they are born from the aforementioned designation-contact, it would be appropriate to call all four mental aggregates 'born of designation-contact' (adhivacanasamphassaja); why then is only perception (saññā) called so? The name that comes to the three mental aggregates by virtue of their nature, when it arises in that perception, the term 'born of designation-contact' becomes well-established (nirūḷhī) and expresses the intrinsic nature; therefore, it is attributed only to that perception, while the others withdraw. For this reason, it is said: 'The three immaterial aggregates...' and so on. Alternatively, since perception has another distinct name, 'born of resistance-contact' (paṭighasamphassaja), the name 'born of designation-contact' should belong only to the remaining three aggregates. However, those three aggregates give their name to perception and withdraw; intending this meaning, it is said: 'The three immaterial aggregates...' and so on. The fact that perception occurring in the five doors can be known just by looking is like the intimation (viññatti) which is the cause for knowing an intention when making hand gestures and so on with various desires; looking, which is the cause for knowing lust and so on in acts like looking with lust, becomes manifest when the object and the eye-consciousness meet. Perception associated with that looking is also said to be manifest in that way. To prevent the doubt that perception manifest through looking with lust and so on should occur in impulsion (javana), it is said: 'It has only a sensitive base (pasādavatthu).' 'One who thinks of another' means one who is thinking of something other than what was previously thought or known by him. ## The explanation of the aggregate of perception is finished. ## 4. Explanation of the Aggregate of Volitional Formations 'By the lower limit' (heṭṭhimakoṭiyā)—here it is merely a designation by the locative case. This is because volition (cetanā), which is predominant in that lower limit of the arising of consciousness, is shown. If this is so, does it not follow that it is not shown in the upper limit? It does not follow, because there can be no state of reaching the lower limit without the state of reaching the upper limit. For the lower limit is all-pervading. In the second instance of the word 'heṭṭhimakoṭiyā', it is a designation by the instrumental case, and should be connected as 'those coming by way of the lower limit.' Or, in the previous instance as well, what was said as 'by the lower limit' is a designation by the instrumental case because it is stated by way of showing the predominant formation (saṅkhāra). By the Pali 'formations associated with that volition', the forty-nine types of formations are meant. These formations are already included because they are bound to that volition. ## The explanation of the aggregate of volitional formations is finished.
17:
## Explanation of the Miscellaneous Discussion (*Pakiṇṇakakathā*)

The word *samuggama* is well-known in the senses of "arising together" and "initial arising". When there is a combination of various conditions such as ignorance, craving, and kamma, the arising by ascending from the previous end, known as the previous life, is *samuggama*. Alternatively, the arising of the aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is *samuggama*. That *samuggama* is shown only in the five-constituent existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) where the five aggregates arise completely. By this method, the arising of aggregates in the one-constituent (*ekavokāra*) and four-constituent (*catuvokāra*) existences, where aggregates are incomplete, can also be understood. Or else, the simultaneous arising of all five aggregates as they are obtained is *samuggama*. In this sense, the incomplete arising is not included. The wool of a noble-bred sheep in the Himālayan region is called *jāti-uṇṇā*. In the term "drop of ghee-cream" (*sappimaṇḍabindu*), the word *bindu* (drop) should also be applied and understood. "Having such a color-counterpart" (*evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāga*) means a group of matter having such a color and such a shape. Or, *paṭibhāga* means attaining similarity. Because there is similarity in terms of such color and shape, it is called "having such a color-counterpart".

"Heads of continuity" (*santatisīsāni*) means the roots of the continuity of matter, or the portions of the continuity of matter. Just as the principal limb is called the "head" because it is a collection of many faculties (*indriya*), so the portions such as the heart-decad (*vatthu-dasaka*) and so on, which are clusters of many types of matter, are called "heads".

The statement "the five aggregates are complete" is said with reference to the completeness of the number of the five aggregates; it does not mean the completeness of each individual aggregate. Since the continuity of matter produced by kamma is mentioned, it might be said that the continuity produced by temperature (*utu*), mind (*citta*), and nutriment (*āhāra*) occurs after such a time, etc. However, because that matter will be discussed in the section "by way of priority and posteriority" (*pubbāparatoti*), it is not mentioned yet. To show the continuity of kamma-born matter that has not yet been mentioned, the spontaneous arising (*opapātika-samuggama*) is shown. Thus, by the words "the five aggregates are complete", the method is shown by way of spontaneous beings (*opapātika*) whose sense-bases (*āyatana*) are complete. For spontaneous beings in the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) whose sense-bases are incomplete, the deficiency of the heads of continuity should be understood by way of their deficient sense-bases.

This investigation "by way of priority and posteriority" (*pubbāparatoti*) should be understood as applying not to the arising of the five aggregates, but only to their production of matter (*rūpasamuṭṭhāpane*). Desiring to show this meaning, he said "But thus..." (*evaṃ pana*) and so on. By the words "among those arisen without priority or posteriority", he shows the cause of doubt. Among the five aggregates that arise together, if it is not shown that "this state alone produces matter first, and this one later", it is not easy to know. Here, the five aggregates that arise and occur at the moment of rebirth-linking are taken as the basis for this investigation "by way of priority and posteriority". In that taking...
18:
Because it is indicated by the locative case in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa), the author of the Saṅgaha stated, "Matter first causes matter to arise." Alternatively, if it were indicated by the locative case in the sense of a state characterized by another state (bhāvena bhāva lakkhaṇa), then at the moment matter causes matter to arise, it should also be said that kamma causes matter to arise; thus, it would be proper to say "both [mind and matter]." This investigation is carried out by taking the continuity of matter and the continuity of mind into account; therefore, it is said, "Matter first causes matter to arise." Otherwise, if the investigation were conducted by taking only the mind and matter present at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), then since the mind's ability to cause matter to arise does not yet exist, it would have to be said that the investigation of causing [matter] to arise in succession is not applicable at this moment of rebirth-linking.

The statement "The base-matter (vatthu-rūpa) is weak at the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa)" was made with reference to the lack of strength of all matter at the moment of arising. Indeed, at that moment of arising, that matter is said to be "weak" because it is devoid of the post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) and is not supported by conditions such as nutriment (āhāra).

The phrase "Because it is impelled by the force of kamma (kammavega)" was said with reference to this meaning: although the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arises due to kamma, that resultant continuity at the moment of rebirth-linking is as if impelled by a kamma other than the one that causes the preceding life-continuum to arise, and thus it is not firmly established; however, after that moment of rebirth-linking, it becomes established in a similar continuity by obtaining the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) and the pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya).

"The continuity is connected" means that the continuity of the base-matter, such as the eye-base, performs the connection by way of the arising of another base-matter while one base-matter is still present; it does not have a break in its occurrence like the bases that are the supports for death (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). "From the factors" means from the jhana factors (jhānaṅga). Indeed, the jhana factors, together with the mind, cause matter to arise; the path factors (maggaṅga) and others provide corresponding strength to those jhana factors, because the occurrence of specific matter is seen when those jhana and path factors are present. Alternatively, the mental factors such as volition (cetanā), which are factors of the mind, reach the state of being a factor or an associate in the mind's production of matter; the meaning is that they cause matter to arise only when they are not deficient in the jhana factors and others that provide strength to those factors like volition. Because they are deficient in those jhana factors, minds such as eye-consciousness do not cause matter to arise.

If someone were to say, "Let the base-matter that arises together with the rebirth-linking mind cause matter to arise during the static (ṭhiti) and dissolution (bhaṅga) moments of that rebirth-linking mind, because it is a pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya) and thus the cause known as pre-nascence condition is not lacking," the author stated "Yadi hi cittaṃ" etc., wishing to refute that person's claim. In that statement, he conceded that it should not be said that the base-matter of those mental states cannot be a pre-nascence condition at the static and dissolution moments; however, even while conceding that, he showed the fault therein. If it could cause matter to arise at that time, then according to your view, the rebirth-linking mind should also be able to cause it; but in fact, at that time, there is no production of matter at all. And when there is the production of matter, at the moment of arising, even according to your view, the cause is indeed deficient because there is no pre-nascence support (purejāta-nissaya) at the moment of rebirth-linking; therefore, the rebirth-linking mind cannot cause matter to arise—this is the intention here. At the moment of arising, the eight types of matter...
19:
...taking the eight types of matter at the moment of arising, it causes them to occur. Why? Because mental states arise with impetus and full strength due to the power of conditions such as the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya).

"Avisayatāya" means because it is not the domain of a new guest who has arrived at a village where he has never been before. "Appahutatāya" means because that new guest has no authority in that village. The statement "Cittasamuṭṭhāna... pe... ṭhitāni" was made considering that just as the mind and mental factors benefit the mind-produced matter through modes (powers) such as nutriment (āhāra) and faculty (indriya), so too at the time of rebirth-linking, the mind and mental factors benefit the thirty types of kamma-produced matter exactly as they should through all those modes.

"The root of the round" (vaṭṭamūla) refers to craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā). The matter that arises due to the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) does not continue to arise in another existence like the matter that arises due to the minds preceding that death-consciousness. Therefore, because the root of the round has been extinguished, the non-arising of matter should be investigated.

The statement "Rūpassa natthitāya" was made with reference to the absence of matter to be produced, because the immaterial jhana (arūpa-jhāna) is the means of escape from matter, and because matter has already been abandoned through the power of dispassion (virāga). Otherwise, in an existence where matter occurs, because there is basic matter, the mental states which are the causes of matter can produce matter. The immaterial realm (arūpa-bhava), however, is not a location for matter. Therefore, if there were basic matter, the mind could produce other matter; the meaning is that even that basic matter does not exist in that immaterial realm. In truth, the beneficial nature of previously arisen matter also exists; this is known from seeing the similarity of the children's physical form to that of their parents.

Temperature (utu), however, causes matter to arise first because it causes matter to arise at the static moment (ṭhitikkhaṇa) of the rebirth-linking mind—this is the commentator's intention. The statement beginning with "Utu nāma cesa dandhanirodho" was made to show the reason for the production of matter at the static moment of temperature and to show the time when mental states produce matter. Indeed, because temperature is slow to cease (dandhanirodha), it is strong at that static moment and thus can produce matter. While that temperature-produced matter is still present, when sixteen minds which are quick to cease have arisen, the first life-continuum (bhavaṅga) immediately following the rebirth-linking mind again causes matter to arise within the matter produced by temperature—this is the meaning. While that temperature-produced matter is still present, sixteen minds arise and cease. By this statement, if the arising and dissolution moments of temperature are taken within the static moment itself, it would mean "matter has a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments." If the arising moment is not taken and only the dissolution moment is taken, it would mean "it has a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments." If the dissolution moment is not taken and only the arising moment is taken, it would mean "it has a lifespan of more than sixteen mind-moments." If neither the arising nor the dissolution moments are taken, it would mean "it has a lifespan of more than seventeen mind-moments." However, since the rebirth-linking mind is also included among the minds occurring during the static moment of that temperature by the text "tesu paṭisandhianantaraṃ," the arising moment is already taken within the static moment. Thus, if the dissolution moment is not taken, the phrase "adhika-soḷasa" (more than sixteen) which will be mentioned later...
20:
In the phrase “paṭisandhianantaraṃ,” the rebirth-linking consciousness is also included (by way of inclusion) among the consciousnesses that arise during the presence (thiti) of that temperature (utu). Therefore, since the arising moment (uppāda) is taken within the moment of presence, if the dissolution moment (nirodha) is not taken, it should be understood as referring to a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments along with the excess to be mentioned; or if the dissolution moment is taken, it refers to a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments.

The phrase “ojā kharā” is spoken with reference to the nutritive essence (ojā) together with its physical basis (vatthu). This is because the nutritive essence, which is subtle by nature, possesses the qualities of coarseness or subtlety by virtue of its physical basis.

The phrase “cittañceva” is stated because consciousness is the precursor (the primary factor). In reality, however, the mental factors (cetasikas) associated with that consciousness also produce matter (rūpa). This is in accordance with the teaching: “Root-condition (hetu-paccaya) is a condition for the states associated with the roots and for the matter produced by them by way of root-condition,” and so forth. Alternatively, by the word “citta,” the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda), which is a collection of consciousness and mental factors, is taken. It does not refer to a single state that is not manifest, like kamma-volition (kamma-cetanā). If it is asked, “Should matter originated by kamma also be produced by the mental factors associated with that kamma?” No, it should not. This is because it is not taught that they are produced by those factors, and because those states associated with kamma do not serve as a condition for that matter by any means.

“Addhānaparicchedato” means by way of the limitation of duration (time). In this context, it refers to the limitation of duration such that “seventeen mind-moments are the duration of matter, and one-seventeenth of the duration of matter is the duration of the immaterial (nāma).” The phrase “paṭisandhikkhaṇe” should be understood as merely an illustration of the method. This is because the co-occurrence of matter and the immaterial is also evident after the moment of rebirth-linking. However, it should be noted that this statement is not made with the intention that there is no co-occurrence at the moment of rebirth-linking. The commentator himself will state that matter arises even during the moments of presence (thiti) and dissolution (bhaṅga) of the rebirth-linking consciousness. By the illustration of the bearing of fruit, the difference in duration between matter and the immaterial is shown. It does not show their co-arising, as it was not intended to show that co-arising. In fact, because the difference in duration can be easily demonstrated through co-arising, the mention of co-arising is made solely for the purpose of that demonstration.

If so, since the durations of matter and the immaterial are unequal, would it not follow that matter could exist apart from the immaterial? To prevent this objection, the phrase beginning with “tattha kiñcāpi” is stated. “Ekapamāṇā vā” is said considering that among the material and immaterial states occurring without interruption, there is no matter without the immaterial, nor any immaterial without matter. This statement should be understood as referring to the occurrence of kamma-born matter in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), excluding the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) which is similar to Nibbāna. “Pade padaṃ” means stepping quickly as if placing the hind foot exactly in the previous footprint. “Anohāya” means without leaving (occurring together) until death (cuti).
21:
It should be understood that [the author of the Saṅgaha] has composed this with reference to the occurrence of kamma-born materiality (kammaja-rūpa) in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhūmi), excluding the moment of the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), which is similar to Nibbāna. The meaning is to step quickly, as if placing the hind foot exactly where or near where the front foot was placed. As long as there is death (cuti), there is a continuous occurrence without abandonment until that death. However, at the moment of death (cuti-khana), it should be noted that materiality and mentality cease together. The period during which they occur without abandoning each other is, at most, the duration (addhā) delimited by rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and death (cuti), which is the time of occurrence for these material and mental phenomena. It should be understood that with the word 'evaṃ' (thus), [the author of the Saṅgaha] includes both the previously mentioned inferior duration and this superior duration delimited by rebirth-linking and death.

It should be understood that [the author of the Saṅgaha] has taken this pair together as 'ekuppāda-nānānirodhato' (arising together but ceasing differently), which is a mode to be contemplated through the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā) regarding materiality and mentality. The same applies to the subsequent matrix (mātikā) terms. Some teachers say that the phrase 'pacchimakammajaṃ ṭhapetvā' (excluding the last kamma-born materiality) was stated by [the author of the Saṅgaha] considering that since the last kamma-born materiality ceases together with the death-consciousness, there is no 'different cessation' (nānā-nirodha). However, that kamma-born materiality also does not have a 'common arising' (ekuppāda) with the consciousness, because it was stated below that it arises at the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-khana) of the last of the sixteen consciousnesses. If a consciousness that lacks both common arising and different cessation should be excluded, then all kamma-born materiality arising at the moment of dissolution of any consciousness should also be excluded. However, since kamma-born materiality no longer arises while consciousnesses continue to occur after the moment the last kamma-born materiality arises, there is no kamma-born materiality to be avoided or taken at that time. Therefore, it should be understood that 'pacchimakammajaṃ ṭhapetvā' was stated.

Prior to the time of the last kamma-born materiality, there is a succession of forty-eight kamma-born materialities. In that commentary, whichever kamma-born materiality arises at the moment of arising (uppāda-khana) of a consciousness, that kamma-born materiality ceases at the moment of arising of another consciousness. Therefore, it should be noted that by taking 'ekuppāda-nānānirodhaṃ' and excluding the materialities arising at the moments of presence (ṭhī-khana) and dissolution (bhaṅga-khana), the connection of meaning was made such that [the five aggregates] are to be known through common arising and different cessation in the manner described. That kamma-born materiality has common arising and different cessation with mentality, and mentality has the same with that kamma-born materiality. In that context, considering the succession (paveṇī) like the links of a chain, the statement was made regarding the succession connected with forty-eight kamma-born materialities. If taken by another method, a statement regarding the succession connected with forty-nine kamma-born materialities should be made.

The phrase 'nānuppāda...pe... pacchimakammajena dīpetabbā' was stated because it can be easily demonstrated by the last kamma-born materiality. It is easily demonstrated by that last kamma-born materiality. This is because, by the method shown in this last kamma-born materiality, even prior to that, materiality arising at the moment of dissolution of one consciousness ceases exactly at the moment of dissolution of another consciousness. Therefore, it is because that prior kamma-born materiality can be known to have different arising (nānuppāda) and common cessation (ekanirodha) with mentality, and mentality with that prior kamma-born materiality. In both the time of the last kamma-born materiality and the time of the materiality prior to it, materiality that arises at the moment of presence of one consciousness and will cease at the moment of presence of another subsequent consciousness, and mentality that arises at the moment of presence of that materiality and will cease at the moment of presence of that same materiality, have not yet been included. It should be understood that those material and mental phenomena come to be included in this very matrix (mātikā) as 'nānuppādato nānānirodhato' (different arising and different cessation). It should be noted that the demonstration of the state of different arising and different cessation by means of materiality included in the four successions of materiality is a demonstration of the method by the power of the different arising and different cessation materiality that has not yet been shown, because the materiality arising at the moment of presence has already been shown in this section. Death can occur for a being in the womb who is established in exactly thirty kamma-born materialities. Therefore, the last kamma-born materiality has also been connected in relation to those kamma-born materialities.

Why should there be those who do not die? Just as the arising of the six base-materialities (vatthu-rūpa) such as the eye is due to kamma, the arising of mental resultants (vipāka) such as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) which depend on those six base-materialities should also be due to the very kamma that causes those base-materialities to arise. Among those kamma-born material and mental phenomena, there is no reason to distinguish that some arise while others do not.
22:
Why would there be those who do not die? Because by the very same kamma that produces those six physical bases (vatthu-rūpa), the occurrence of resultant mental states (vipāka-nāma) such as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), which depend on those six bases, should also occur. For there is no reason why that kamma should produce some of those kamma-born phenomena and not others. Therefore, since the life-constituents (jīvita-saṅkhāra) such as vitality (āyu), heat (usmā), and consciousness (viññāṇa) are not deficient, it is said, "There would be those who do not die."

"Matter that arises at the arising sub-moment (uppāda-kkhaṇa) of a preceding mind ceases at the arising sub-moment of the seventeenth subsequent mind; matter that arises at the static sub-moment (ṭhiti-kkhaṇa) ceases at the static sub-moment of the seventeenth subsequent mind; matter that arises at the dissolving sub-moment (bhaṅga-kkhaṇa) ceases at the dissolving sub-moment of the seventeenth subsequent mind." This statement is meant to be said because it appears in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). However, his own view is shown thus: matter arising at the arising sub-moment ceases at the dissolving sub-moment; matter arising at the static sub-moment ceases at the arising sub-moment; and matter arising at the dissolving sub-moment ceases at the static sub-moment. By doing so, it is stated in the section on the delimitation of duration (addhāna-pariccheda) that "that matter ceases together with the seventeenth mind." This statement contradicts this Pāḷi text. Why? Because the lifespan of matter produced by the four causes should also be equal. For whatever reason these teachers have combined them, for that reason, the state of matter having simultaneous arising but different cessation, and the state of having different arising but simultaneous cessation, simply cannot exist.

These teachers state that matter has a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments (cittakkhaṇa). However, in the Commentary, it is stated to have a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments and one sub-moment (one-third of a moment). That statement contradicts the lifespan of sixteen mind-moments shown in the Vibhaṅga Commentary on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda-vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā), which, in order to show rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) with a present object immediately after death (cuti) with a past object, states: "By this much, eleven mind-moments have passed; likewise, fifteen mind-moments have passed; then, rebirth-linking consciousness arises with that very same object which has a remaining lifespan of five mind-moments or one mind-moment." It is not possible to say, "Matter comes into focus (āpāthamāgacchati) only at the static sub-moment (ṭhiti-kkhaṇa)." If that were so, it would not be that eleven or fifteen mind-moments of matter have passed, but rather more than eleven or fifteen mind-moments would have passed. Therefore, even if it were granted that only matter which has reached the static stage strikes the sensitive material (pasāda) in the five-door process, in the mind-door process (mano-dvāra), it must be accepted that it comes into focus even at the arising sub-moment (uppāda-kkhaṇa). For it is not that any object, such as a past one, cannot come into focus in the mind-door; indeed, it can.
