If some were to say that mental distress (domanassa) itself is despair (upāyāsa), they should be refuted by this Dhātukathā Pali: "Despair is associated with three aggregates, one base, and one element; it is associated in some ways with one aggregate, one base, and one element" (Dhatuk. 249). For those who, having reached despondency, stand in misery without considering the causes of happiness or suffering, despair is the cause of physical suffering. For those who think of the destruction of relatives and so on by the power of despondency, it is the cause of mental distress. At the moment of its own occurrence, despair consumes the mind because it is associated with mental distress; it causes the body to sink by making it inactive. Because it performs both these functions, it subsequently generates excessive physical and mental suffering based on that cause; thus it is called "suffering" (dukkha).

## Explanation of the Description of Association with the Unloved (Appiyasampayoganiddesavaṇṇanā)
"Na appiyanti" means they are not approached, they are not entered. "Anattha" means destruction or suffering. "Ahita" means the cause of that destruction. In the second interpretation of the meaning, because one does not desire the growth of welfare, the term "anatthakāma" (desiring harm) and such improper compounds (asamatthasamāsa) should also be applied.
67:
In words such as "anatthakāma," an improper compound (asamatthasamāsa) with an unsuitable meaning is also applied. Just as in words like "asūriyapassāni mukhāni" (faces that do not see the sun), the "a-" prefix does not negate the word it is compounded with. In the sense of being free from any specific danger, the word "yogakkhema" is well-known because it is security (khema) due to being free from the yoke of suffering (dukkha-yoga).

In words like "saṅgati" (association), whatever meaning can be obtained by the power of formations (saṅkhāra) should be taken. Since formations do not have postures such as standing or sitting, nor do they act together in activities like eating, it cannot be said that the latter two terms (samodhāna and missībhāva) are obtained by the power of that meaning. "Yaṃ labbhati" means whatever meaning is obtained. Therefore, just as the meaning is obtained in words like "saṅgati," it should be applied in that manner. For a person, "saṅgati" is going and associating with formations, and associating with those formations that have come; it is the coexistence of a person with formations in his own postures like standing, and the mixing in all activities. "Anatthabhāva" is the state of being a calamity (upaddava).

The mere approach of undesirable beings and formations, and the mere grasping of that undesirable object, is called "association with the unloved" (appiyasampayoga). However, there is no single distinct state called "association with the unloved" like the states of earth (pathavī) or contact (phassa); thus it is said, "In terms of ultimate reality, it is not a single distinct state." Undesirable formations like thorns and so on, and enemies, produce suffering such as being pierced by arrows and so on.

The word "idha" (here) should be applied as "suffering occurs in this world," or "it is called suffering here in this description of the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca-niddesa)."

## Explanation of the Description of Separation from the Loved (Piyavippayoganiddesavaṇṇanā)
"Minanti" means they put inside, like putting grain into a measuring vessel; it means they do not put it outside. The word "amā" indicates coexistence. Or they are known as "insiders" (ajjhattika). Because it arises in the mind as the ruin of relatives (ñātibyasana) and so on, it is called "manifesting as ruin" (byasanapaccupaṭṭhāna). By causing sorrow, they dry up the body and make it thin; even if not thin, they make it wither by removing its vitality (ojā). Because of that withering, physical suffering arises; thus it is said that they are the producers of that physical suffering.

By the phrase "pierced by the arrow of sorrow" (sokasarasamappitā), mental suffering is shown; by the phrase "they are tormented" (vitujjanti), physical suffering is shown.
68:
## Explanation of the Description of Desire (Icchā-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

Since the intended meaning is the non-coming of birth (*jāti*) that occurs in those who have attained *Parinibbāna*, the phrase "the non-coming of birth that occurs in those who have attained *Parinibbāna*" is stated by taking the time when rebirth (*jāti*) cannot come. The meaning of the word "*yampi*" is "*yena pi*" (because of which also). Alternatively, when the word "*yaṃ*" refers to the word "*icchā*" (desire), it expresses a desire characterized by non-attainment. However, when it refers to the word "*na labhati*" (does not get), it expresses a non-attainment characterized by desire. Although that non-attainment has no other ultimate reality (*dhamma*) than greed (*lobha*), it refers only to the craving (*taṇhā*) that desires what should not be obtained. Because it occurs in things that cannot be obtained, it is called "*appatti-paccupaṭṭhāna*" (manifesting as non-attainment). The reason is that such desire occurs in a certain object, and it is perceived (by knowledge) as being unable to reach that object.

"*Chinnabhinnagaṇena*" means either by a group of shameless rogues or by a group of wretched people wearing rags.

"*Vighātamayaṃ*" refers to mental distress (*domanassa*) consisting of mental exhaustion/vexation, and also to physical suffering (*dukkha*) such as hanging oneself, illness, dysentery, etc., which arise from that very mental exhaustion. By the word "*icchitālābhaṃ*", the desire for an unobtainable object is meant.

## Explanation of the Description of the Aggregates of Clinging (Upādānakkhandha-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

Showing the vast suffering as "having this much extent" is the summarization of suffering; such summarization cannot be done [exhaustively] because the extension of suffering is infinite. However, setting aside the extension of the teaching (*desanā*) that has reached the vastness of suffering, the defining of the teaching at the point where all extensions of suffering converge is called summarization; such summarization can be done because the objects known as the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*) clearly exist.

Just as a man who knows a region and shows the way is called a "*desaka*" (shower/pointer), the Blessed One is also a "*desaka*" who points out suffering. There is also a variant reading "*dukkhantadesakena*", which means one who teaches the end of suffering.

Just as fire and so on oppress fuel and so on, they [the aggregates] arise while oppressing. By this very obvious suffering called "the oppression of suffering occurring at the time of death," the Buddha shows the sufferings such as sorrow (*soka*) caused by the oppression of the suffering of birth (*jāti*) and the suffering of aging (*jarā*). "*Tato*" refers to the suffering of oppression (*ābādhana-dukkha*) that occurs after lamentation (*parideva*). The bodily suffering that severely oppresses the body due to the conjunction of the disturbance of elements (*dhātu*) which causes dryness of the throat, the breaking of joints and ligaments, etc., is called "*dukkha*" (bodily pain). "*Yesu kesuci*" means that all sufferings such as eye disease, etc., occurring in the aggregates of clinging of Tissa or Phussa, or in all beings, are only of this nature, categorized into the five aggregates of clinging; this is the meaning intended to be shown in summary.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Truth of Suffering is finished.
69:
## 2. Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Origin (Samudayasacca-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

By eliding the latter word '*karaṇa*', it is said: "*punabbhavakaraṇaṃ punobbhavo*" (it is called *punobbhava* because it makes for renewed existence). In the word "*manosamphasso*", the ending in 'o' of the preceding word should be understood as in the word '*mano*'. Alternatively, since it has the meaning known by the suffix '*ika*' which has the sense of habit (*sīla*), it should be understood that the word expressing the action is not shown. For example, one who has the habit of eating cake is called "*āpūpiko*". The formation of the word '*ponobbhavika*' should be understood in meanings such as "it gives renewed existence" (*punabbhavāṃ deti*) because of the plural designation "*taddhitā*", because of the diversity of *taddhita* suffixes, or because they have the characteristic of expressing the meaning of a sentence.

Among those cravings (*taṇhā*), the craving that co-arises with *kamma* gives renewed existence. The craving that is a companion to *kamma* but does not co-arise with that *kamma* leads to renewed existence. Both types cause birth in existence again and again. Therefore, it is said: "*punabbhavassa dāyikāpi*" (being a giver of renewed existence), and so on. Regarding the phrase "it receives the name *ponobbhavika*": both the craving that can give renewed existence and the craving that cannot give it receive the same name '*ponobbhavika*' as having the same result. This is because they have the same nature in terms of longing for existence and because they have the power to give that existence. The same should be understood for the remaining cravings. Among those cravings, the *kamma* that ripens in the individual existence (*attabhāva*) already produced by other *kamma* called '*upadhi*' belongs to this craving; therefore, it is called "*upadhivepakkā*". It is called '*nandī*' in the sense of delighting; it is called '*rāgo*' in the sense of lusting. Whatever delight-and-lust (*nandīrāga*) and whatever craving (*taṇhā*) there are, these two are the same in meaning and differ only in phrasing; thus craving is said to be "identical in meaning with delight-and-lust." Because of the connection with lust (*rāga*), it is said "*uppannassa*" (of the arisen). Since the lust for fine-material existence and immaterial existence will be mentioned separately, it should be understood that the arising of craving that longs for existence only in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) is mentioned here.

It is said "*uppajjati*" (arises) by way of the first arising in various pleasant objects, and "*nivisati*" (settles/establishes) by way of repeated occurrence. Alternatively, the arising and settling should be applied by way of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) and underlying tendency (*anusaya*). "*Sampattiyaṃ*" means it occurs in human prosperity and in the state of being a deity. "*Attano cakkhu*" refers to the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhu-pasāda*) together with its physical base, or the eyeball together with the sensitivity. "*Vippasannapañcapasādaṃ*" refers to the sensitivity having very pure colors of blue, yellow, red, black, and white. Because the interior is white, they perceive the ear-hole like a silver tube. They perceive it like a hanging thread tied to a pendulous earlobe. A nose that is both high and long is called '*tunganāsikā*'; [people cherish] their own nose which has gained such a designation. Alternatively, if the reading is "*laddhavohārā*", it means those who have a high nose are called '*tunganāsikā*'; beings who have gained such a designation [cherish] their own nose—this is how the meaning should be applied. They also perceive the tongue by way of color, shape, and function. They perceive the mind as a noble mind capable of investigating matters such as the past. "*Attanā paṭiladdhāni*" means those obtained within one's own internal continuity...
70:
Smells of the body and external scents such as perfumes and ointments [are connected to the fourfold-originated base of smell, etc.]. In the phrase 'it arises while it is arising,' when it is in the process of arising, it arises here in this eye; thus, the act of arising taken generally is stated as the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), and the act of arising distinguished by its locus is stated as the object to be characterized (lakkhitabba). It is not that there is no conventional usage distinguished by generality and specificity (it indeed exists). Alternatively, 'arising' (uppajjamānā) refers to the undecided act of arising stated as the cause. 'Arises' (uppajjati) refers to the decided act of arising stated as the result, as in 'if it is in the process of arising, it arises in this eye.' That act of arising is as if it were joined with the process of arising.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Origin is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Description of the Truth of Cessation

'Anūhata' means not uprooted, not abandoned.

A lion acts against the shooter, not the arrow; a dog acts against the stone, not the thrower. [Craving] is dispassionate through the power of reaching exhaustion. It ceases through the power of reaching non-occurrence. It is abandoned through the power of giving up without regard and through the power of decrease. It is relinquished through the power of throwing far away so that it cannot occur again. It is released through the power of liberation from craving, which is a bond. It does not cling through the power of being without defilement. Accumulation is the origin (samudaya); non-accumulation through the power of its opposite is [cessation].

'Apaññatti' means reaching non-manifestation, or the absence of the conventional expression 'the bitter gourd exists.' The Path should be understood like a man who desires the non-occurrence of the bitter gourd vine. Just as that man, with a mind inclined toward the non-occurrence of that vine, cuts the root, so the Path, having Nibbāna as its object, abandons craving. Nibbāna should be understood as the non-occurrence of craving, like the non-occurrence of that vine. In the second simile, Nibbāna should be understood like the south gate (or the area near the south gate), and the Path like the executioners. Alternatively, the previous simile was stated to show that craving, which has ceased because of the Path, should be said to have ceased in pleasant and agreeable things. The latter simile was stated to show that it is also said to have ceased in pleasant and agreeable things even though it has ceased by taking Nibbāna as its object.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Truth of Cessation is finished.
71:
## 4. Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Path

'Aññamagga-paṭikkhepanattha' means to reject the fact that the path devised by sectarians is not the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Alternatively, rejecting the status of being a path for other practices is called 'rejecting other paths' (aññamagga-paṭikkhepa).

It is called 'Noble' (Ariya) because it makes a person reach the state of a Noble One. It is called 'Noble' because it causes the attainment of, or produces, the fruit of a Noble One. It should be understood that this refers only to obtaining the name 'Noble' through the power of its own function and through the power of the fruit. One should understand the formation of the word 'Aṭṭhaṅgika' (Eightfold) as 'the eight factors exist in this path,' without making it a compound where the meaning is external (aññapadattha-samāsa).

Speech endowed with four factors embraces the people. Right Speech (Sammā-vācā), which has the nature of abstinence from the opposite wrong speech, is said to have the 'characteristic of embracing' (pariggaha-lakkhaṇā) because, by abandoning wrong speech that causes division, it has the function of embracing those who hear it and the associated states. Just as work such as making robes brings about a task to be done, or the 'action' (kammanta) called volition (cetanā) which completes various actions brings about movements such as those of hands and feet, so Right Action (Sammā-kammanta), by abandoning wrong action that brings about blameworthy tasks, has the function of bringing about blameless deeds. It is said to have the 'characteristic of originating' (samuṭṭhāpana-lakkhaṇo) because it occurs only while originating the associated states. Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva) is said to have the 'characteristic of purifying' (vodāpana-lakkhaṇo) because it abandons wrong livelihood, which is a defilement of the body, speech, and the continuum of the aggregates.

Its own opposing defilements are ignorance (avijjā) and so on, which are abandoned along with [wrong] view. 'Passatīti' means 'pakāseti' (it manifests/clarifies). For by that factor (Right View), reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā) occurs therein. 'Tatheva' means 'together with its own opposing defilements.'

'Kiccato' (by way of function) is because the task to be performed by the knowledges of suffering, etc., which occur in the preliminary stage, is completed at this moment of the Path. Or, it is because of the function of this Right View knowledge itself in clarifying suffering, etc. It receives three names because of the completion of the function of abandoning sensual thought (kāma-saṅkappa) and so on. In the Vibhaṅga of the Precepts (Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga), it is stated that 'abstinence-volitions and all associated states are precepts'; therefore, by the power of the abstinence-volitions which are primary among those three, it is said that 'there are both abstinences and volitions.' Abstinences should be applied at the time of abstaining from false speech, etc., and volitions should be applied at the time of speaking well-spoken words, etc. At the moment of the Path...
72:
Because they are not factors of the Path, volitions (cetanā) are not path factors; only abstinences (virati) are path factors. It should be understood that only abstinences are path factors because a single knowledge is like the state of knowing suffering etc., and a single abstinence is like the state of abstaining from false speech etc.; whereas a single volition does not have the nature of accomplishing the triad of functions such as Right Speech etc., and thus cannot attain the state of Right Speech etc.; and even if it were to attain the state of Right Speech etc., it could not attain the state of being the three factors.

Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi) occurs both in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga) and at the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇa). Although Right Concentration is extensively analyzed by way of the four jhānas through the power of applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and equanimity (upekkhā), which are aids to concentration, a single concentration cannot accomplish the concentration-function of all four jhānas, just as effort (vāyāma) accomplishes the fourfold function of effort such as preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, and mindfulness (sati) accomplishes the fourfold function of mindfulness such as abandoning the perception of beauty in the body etc., which are unattractive (asubha), painful (dukkha), impermanent (anicca), and non-self (anatta). Therefore, just as the jhāna-concentration in the first jhāna concentration-consciousness in the preliminary stage is only the first jhāna concentration, so it is at the moment of the Path. Similarly, just as the jhāna-concentration in the fourth jhāna concentration-consciousness in the preliminary stage is only the fourth jhāna concentration, so it is at the moment of the Path.

Applied thought (vitakka), which assists vocal utterance, also assists Right Speech (Sammā-vācā) which prevents blameworthy vocal utterance and causes blameless vocal utterance to arise; therefore, he said "Svāyaṃ" etc. Speech that regulates vocal utterance assists Right Action (Sammā-kammanta) which regulates bodily action. "Idaṃ vīriyaṃ" refers to the four Right Exertions (Sammā-ppadhāna). "Gatiyo" means accomplishments or natures such as functions. "Samanvesitvā" means having investigated and reflected.

The connection should be made as: "having learned the two preceding truths, namely the Truth of Suffering (Dukkha-sacca) and the Truth of the Origin (Samudaya-sacca)." By the phrase "iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ" (desirable and lovely), he shows the inclination towards the Truth of Cessation (Nirodha-sacca) and the Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca), not delight (abhinandana). The very inclination towards those truths should be understood as the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) in that context.

"Kiccato" (by way of function) means by way of functions such as full understanding (pariññā) etc. "Ārammaṇa-paṭivedha" (penetration of the object) refers to the penetration that is realization (sacchikiriyā). Why is it said that "all penetrative knowledge is supramundane"? Is it not true that penetration through learning (uggaha) etc. is also penetration, yet it is not supramundane? No, it is not so. This is because the word "penetration" (paṭivedha) alone is not intended to mean penetration through learning etc., or because the knowledge in the preliminary stage regarding suffering etc., which proceeds by way of learning etc., is called "penetration" because it is a cause for penetration, not because it is penetration itself. However, referring only to knowledge that is actual penetration, he said: "All penetrative knowledge is supramundane." Since knowledges arising from learning and questioning are included only in the knowledge of hearing (savana-ñāṇa), he mentioned only three types of knowledge: "The knowledge of hearing, remembering, and contemplating is mundane." Comprehending the truths through learning etc. is called "pariggaha" (comprehension).
73:
"Payoga" means action or effort (vāyāma). He shows the desirability and the extreme difficulty of that great effort through similes such as "bhavaggagahaṇatthaṃ" (for the sake of grasping the peak of existence) etc.

In this context of "padaghāta", the track or cause of occurrence is called "pada". The means or cause by which sensual thought (kāma-vitakka) arises is its track; the destruction of that is "padaghāta". "Ussukkāpetvā" means having made it endowed with successive higher distinctions of peace, i.e., having increased it.

Regarding "vibhattesu pāḷiyaṃ" (analyzed in the texts), in which texts? First, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 8 kasiṇas, 10 asubhas, 4 brahmavihāras, and 4 āruppas are analyzed. In the Agamas (Suttas), 10 recollections (anussati), the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā), and the analysis of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna) are analyzed in various places. "Imesu tīsu" (in these three) refers to the three instances such as sense-desire (kāma) etc.

By the phrase "known as wrong speech", he shows the unity of what is to be abandoned by a single volition. Here, "ariya-sāvaka" (noble disciple) includes the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) and the trainee (sekkha). "Kāyadvāravītikkaṃā" (transgressions through the body-door) should be applied to the respective abstinences from killing etc., which are rooted in livelihood (ājīva).

"Ayaṃ panassā" refers to taking the fourfold path as a unity by way of being the Path; this is the distinction of this Path by way of jhāna, being entirely similar, entirely dissimilar, or partially similar. "Pādakajjhāna-niyāmena hoti" (it occurs by the rule of the basic jhāna): here, he speaks making the rule of the basic jhāna the primary focus. In the Atthasālinī, however, he speaks making the rule of insight (vipassanā-niyāma) the primary focus, because there it is not in conflict with all doctrines. But here, he mentions the rule of the basic jhāna to exclude the doctrines of the "contemplated jhāna" (sammasita-jjhāna) and the "disposition of the person" (puggalajjhāsaya). The rule of insight, being common to all, should be understood as not being rejected here either. Intending that other teachers' doctrines to be mentioned should also be analyzed, he said "pādakajjhāna-niyāmena tāva" (firstly, by the rule of the basic jhāna) and analyzed the rule of the basic jhāna in detail.

The statement "In the formless realm, the fourfold and fivefold jhāna... is mentioned in the Atthasālinī" is the intention of the commentator. Is it not said there that "In the formless realm, the threefold and fourfold jhāna arises," and not "the fourfold and fivefold jhāna"? True, but by showing the arising of those jhānas about which there is doubt, it is effectively said that the fourfold and fivefold jhāna arises. Thus it should be understood. Considering the group as a whole, he said: "And that is supramundane, not mundane." For only the fourth jhāna arises there as mundane, while the fourfold and fivefold group does not arise as mundane.
74:
In this context, "how" means: how should it be understood in the absence of the base jhana (pādakajjhāna)? It means that for those possessing jhana in that formless realm, the three higher paths arise by making the first fruit and so on the base for the development of the higher paths. When developing the path associated with the threefold or fourfold jhana, for a person born in that formless realm, other paths associated with different jhanas also arise by making the formless jhana and the fruit associated with that jhana the base for the development of the higher paths. Therefore, the preliminary attainment (pubbābhisaṅkhārasamāpatti) that determines the jhana factors and so on is the base; since it is said that the attainment to be contemplated is not the base, the status of the fruit as a base should also be understood.

Because the knowledge of suffering and so on has the six objects such as visible forms, and because thoughts of renunciation (nekkhammasaṅkappa) and so on have various wholesome objects such as kasinas, and because the factors such as right speech have various objects to be abstained from, it is said "according to suitability" (yathānurūpaṃ). "Suitability" means that since virtue (sīla) without remorse is a special cause for effort (vīriya), it refers to the suitability of virtue for effort and its associated states. Since it refers only to the associated states, it was not said "to a person who has stood on the ground of virtue," but "to a person who is standing." "Non-confusion of mind" means the state of the mind being guarded by mindfulness (sati), which is described here as "having a single guard." Therefore, it was said, "Thus... for a person who has a well-established guard of the mind."

The state of knowledge (vijjā) of the insight that exhausts taints (āsavakkhaya) has been mentioned. In the path known as the exhaustion of taints, which is comprised of the three aggregates, the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) is called vijjā. The state of conduct (caraṇa) of virtue and the four jhanas has been mentioned. The remaining two aggregates (the aggregate of virtue and the aggregate of concentration) are called caraṇa. That by which they go to Nibbāna is called a vehicle (yāna). Since insight itself is the vehicle, it is called the vehicle of insight (vipassanāyāna). Virtue is a special cause for concentration, and concentration is a cause for insight. Because it is helpful to tranquility (samatha), the aggregate of virtue is also included in the vehicle of tranquility. While making clear the danger in sensual pleasures through the vehicle of insight, and not abandoning the unworldly bliss of jhana through the vehicle of tranquility, one avoids the wrong paths of the two extremes. Just as wisdom is the opposite of delusion, virtue and concentration are the direct opposites of hatred and greed, as they are to be accomplished through non-hatred and non-greed. Due to the union of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, there is goodness (kalyāṇa) in the beginning, middle, and end. This is because virtue and so on are the beginning, middle, and end of the Dispensation (Sāsana). The Dispensation, comprised of the three aggregates known as the Path and Fruit, in which a person standing in the Path or Fruit is called a Noble One (Ariya), is called the ground of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi).

## The Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Path is finished.
## The Explanation of the Suttanta Classification is finished.
75:
## 2. Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification

206-214. The term "Ariya-sacca" (Noble Truth), when occurring in the Truth of Origin (Samudaya-sacca), applies only to the origin known as craving (taṇhā), which is devoid of the state of being fully known (pariññeyya) and is to be abandoned (pahātabba) exclusively. It does not apply to the remaining defilements and unwholesome states that are both to be abandoned and fully known, nor to the three wholesome roots accompanied by taints (sāsava-kusalamūla) and the remaining wholesome states with taints which are not to be abandoned. Therefore, in that term "Ariya-sacca," the Origin is partial (sappadesa). In the term "Sacca" (Truth) alone, without the word "Ariya," it is without remainder (nippadesa). Therefore, [the commentator] said, "In order to show the Origin without remainder."

The Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Cessation are naturally without remainder (nippadesa) in the teaching of the Noble Truths. This is because there is no other state in the teaching of the Truths that should be called "Suffering" or "Cessation." The Truth of the Path also has no new states in the sections on the eight factors and five factors. Therefore, it is said only of the Origin, "In order to show it without remainder," because that [Origin] is shown as not being new in all three sections. For the purpose of showing the new Truth of Origin, the statement in the teaching of the Truths, "Therein, what is the origin of suffering? It is craving," has the purpose of showing the occurrence of the term "Truth" in craving alone, without involving the unwholesome roots and so on.

By the power of the teaching, the Truth of Suffering by setting aside various origins, the Truth of Cessation by the power of abandoning various origins, and the Truth of the Path by the power of all supramundane wholesome states consisting of eight factors or five factors, are not mentioned in the teaching of the Noble Truths. Therefore, suffering and so on are shown as being partial (with remainder) in that teaching of the Noble Truths. It should be said that the teaching of the Truths (Sacca-desanā) was taught in order to show those states of suffering and so on as being without remainder (nippadesa). "Paccaya-saṅkhātaṃ" means the root cause of suffering such as birth, due to the power of kamma and defilements.

"The Truth of Cessation... is described by five modes"—this shows the distinction of the teaching of the Truths from the teaching of the Noble Truths. Among those five modes, the statement "the abandoning of the three wholesome roots and the remaining wholesome states with taints" should be understood as being taught by the power of abandoning their causes, namely ignorance, craving, and clinging. Or, it should be understood as being taught by the power of their non-occurrence when ignorance and so on are abandoned. This is because wholesome states are not to be abandoned (na hi kusalā pahātabbā). By the word "abandoning" (pahāna), it shows the cessation to be attained by the power of the function of the path. Alternatively, the non-occurrence of craving and so on, which is the nature of cessation itself, should be understood as "abandoning."

Even if, for the purpose of showing the strong support (upanissaya) for the fulfillment of the Noble Eightfold Path at the moment of the supramundane path, [it is said:] "Even before that, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are very pure; when they are thus pure, this Noble Eightfold Path reaches fulfillment in development"...
76:
Although it is taught in this way, the phrase "Even before [the path]" shows the remote supporting condition (dūratarūpanissaya) resulting from the purity of bodily actions and so forth. It also shows the proximate supporting condition (āsannatarūpanissaya) of the five factors such as right view, which arise at the moment of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā). This occurs for the practitioner who dwells frequently contemplating the disadvantages [of formations], being unattached, unjoined, and undeluded regarding the eye and so forth. This happens by way of turning away from all formations as the five aggregates of clinging diminish in the future, by the remoteness of defilements as craving that leads to rebirth is abandoned, and by way of tranquility of body and mind while experiencing physical and mental happiness as the distress, fever, and burning of body and mind are abandoned. This is in accordance with the teaching: "Whatever view such a person has, that is his right view" (M. iii. 431), etc. Thus, it illustrates the occurrence of the teaching on the fivefold path according to the inclination (ajjhāsaya) of individuals who easily understand the fivefold path by way of the proximate supporting condition. Therefore, it was said: "Because of the statement: 'Even before... is perfectly pure,'" and so forth.

In this way, the word "vacanato" (from the statement) in the ablative case is an indicator that makes known the means of the teaching. Alternatively, "vacanato" means that in accordance with His own words, the Blessed One taught that even the fivefold path is indeed the practice (paṭipadā). Where was it taught? In the city of the devas (Devapura). Therefore, to show that method of teaching, the Elders who compiled the Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgāhaka) also pointed out the section on the fivefold path (pañcaṅgika-vāra).

Alternatively, by the very statement "Even before [the path]," which indicates the cause for the specific inclination, it is taught that even the fivefold path is indeed the practice according to the individual's inclination. Therefore, it was said: "Because of the statement: 'Even before... because of the statement... it is taught.'" Thus, it means that the Blessed One also showed the section on the fivefold path in the city of the devas to demonstrate that method taught in the Suttanta.

The entry into the teaching or the entry into meditation (bhāvanā) by way of the jhanas is called "application of jhana" (jhānābhinivesa). It should be understood that the demonstration of four thousand methods in each portion is for the sake of ease in counting. However, according to the way the Pali text stands, it is understood that the flow of the Pali is made by combining five portions each in each practice and in [the sections on] emptiness (suññatā) and so forth. Among those sections, in the eightfold section (aṭṭhaṅgika-vāra), in the second jhana and so forth, the connection should be made as: "At that time, there is a sevenfold path." In the section on the comprehensive inclusion (sabba-saṅgāhika-vāra), the connection should be made according to the nature of the existing phenomena.

## The Explanation of the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya is finished.
77:
## 3. Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā

Why is it said, "As in the previous two [truths]"? Is it not the case that in the exposition of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering in the Suttanta-bhājanīya, the path is taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane? Indeed, in the commentary on that Suttanta-bhājanīya, it is said: "With reference to the arising of knowledge in the preliminary stage by way of learning and so forth regarding the four truths, it is said: 'knowledge of suffering,' etc. However, at the moment of penetration (paṭivedha), there is only a single knowledge." Thus, the mixed mundane and supramundane nature of right view is shown. Likewise, is not the mixed mundane and supramundane nature of right intention and so forth also shown by such passages as: "This so-called right view has various moments and various objects in the preliminary stage; however, at the moment of the path, it has a single moment and a single object"?

This objection is true. Nevertheless, by way of its connection with insight as the cause for the arising of the path, even in that commentary, the Noble Eightfold Path, which is remote from defilements, is shown by taking the demonstration of the meditation on the four truths as the starting point. Because this was done, the nature of the single path-knowledge as "knowledge of suffering" and so forth was extracted by saying: "However, at the moment of penetration, there is only a single knowledge." Also, the nature of intention and so forth associated with the path as "right intention" and so forth was extracted by saying: "At the moment of the path... a single wholesome intention arises; this is called right intention," and so forth. In the Pali text as well, after briefly indicating the eightfold path, "knowledge of suffering" and so forth is stated in order to explain that very path in detail. Because the Noble Eightfold Path was briefly indicated in the Pali and that same path was then explained in detail, in the Suttanta-bhājanīya as well, by this passage "As in the previous two," the mundane nature of the two [truths] (the truth of suffering and the truth of the origin) and the supramundane nature of the [other] two (the truth of cessation and the truth of the path) are stated.

## Explanation of the Question Section is finished.

## Explanation of the Analysis of the Truths is finished.

## 12. Jhānavibhaṅga (Analysis of Jhāna)
## 1. Suttantabhājanīya (Suttanta Classification)
## Mātikāvaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Matrix)
Accomplishment of the preliminary duties (pubbabhāgakaraṇīyasampadā) of jhāna refers to practices such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkhasaṃvara-sīla). Since jhāna on the foul (asubha-jhāna), jhāna on the recollections (anussati-jhāna), and supramundane jhāna (lokuttara-jhāna) do not exist outside this Dispensation (Sāsana), the phrase "in every way" (sabbappakārena) is used to include them all. By the statement, "Other doctrines are empty of recluses," it is shown that even a person accomplished in the preliminary duties that lead to recluseship does not exist outside the Dispensation. Regarding the training rules (sikkhāpadesu) which are taught by way of the mental body (nāmakāya) etc., and which should be practiced by not transgressing the word, or in the sense of the collection of trainings consisting of the volition of restraint (virati-cetanā) that should be fulfilled without transgression—those various trainings such as the bhikkhu-training are parts of the training rules and should be practiced. Thus, it is said that the word "sikkhāpadesu" is an exposition of the states that should be trained in.

In relation to contentment (santoṣa) etc., the following virtues are shown: being satisfied with whatever requisites are obtained, praising the virtue of such contentment, not longing for requisites when they are not obtained, and consuming them without greed when they are obtained. The description of the one who performs the jhāna-meditation is an exposition of the state of being a performer (kārakabhāvapari dīpana). By the word "forest" etc., the types of lodgings (senāsana) are shown; by the word "little noise" etc., the state of being free from faults is shown; and by the word "suitable for seclusion," the benefits (ānisaṃsa) are shown. Thus, it is said, "The types of lodgings... exposition."

## Mātikāvaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā (The Explanation of the Matrix is Finished).

## Niddesavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Exposition)
Because the Dispensation is taught using the word "diṭṭhi" (view) in the sense of an object (kamma-attha), it is said, "It is called diṭṭhi because it is seen," and so on. "Sabhāvaṭṭhena" means in the sense of reality (non-perversion). Only the discipline (vinaya) that is being trained in can discipline the body and so on, and not by any other means; thus it is said, "It is called vinaya in the sense of that which should be trained in." Or else, vinaya is...
177:
The training rules (sikkhāpada) that should be trained in, and the triad of training (sikkhattaya)—the group of virtue, the group of concentration, and the group of wisdom—are called 'Vinaya' because they are like discipline. The three trainings, which constitute the giving of the Teacher's instruction, are referred to as "anusiṭṭhidānavasena" (by way of giving instruction).

"Sammādiṭṭhipaccayattā" means because it is the cause for Right View. This is because Right View becomes fulfilled for one who practices the three trainings. In accordance with the statement, "Therefore, monk, you should first purify the very beginning of wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Well-purified virtue and straight view (diṭṭhi)," the three trainings are preceded by Right View. In these two senses, the three trainings are called "diṭṭhi" by way of metonymy, attributing the name of the effect to the cause (phalūpacāra) and the name of the cause to the effect (kāraṇူpacāra). Alternatively, it is intended to refer to them by way of the wholesome states that are their own parts. The three trainings are called Vinaya because they are the Buddha's act of disciplining. That disciplining occurs through the Dhamma, which is of an even (righteous) nature, or through the Dhamma of the teaching, and not through punishment with a stick etc.; thus it is called "Dhamma-vinaya."

It is for the sake of Nibbāna, which is the supreme faultless state, or for the sake of the unshakable liberation of mind (the fruit of Arahantship). The three trainings, which are the cause for knowing through higher knowledge (abhijñā) etc. regarding the states to be fully known (abhiññeyya) etc., are called "Dhamma-vinaya." The phrase "in this [dispensation]" is repeated to make a definition (limitation) from other dispensations. Alternatively, with the intention that the word "eva" (only) has been elided, it is said, "niyamော kato" (a definition has been made).

In the word "bhikkhuko," the syllable "ka" is added without changing the meaning, thus the meaning is given as "having the nature of begging" (bhikkhana-dhammatā). In the reading "bhikkhako," the meaning is "one who begs." Dirt mixed with dust is called "jallika," while pure dirt without dust is called "mala." Because the word 'bhikkhu' is well-established for a person who wears torn cloth, the definition is given as "bhinnapaṭadhara" (one who wears torn robes).

One for whom there remains a limit (odhi) of the path to be developed and defilements to be abandoned is called "odhiso." An Arahant, however, is without limit (odhirahita) because of the absence of such remainder. Therefore, it is said, "A bhikkhu is anodhiso due to the abandoning of defilements." Alternatively, the word "odhi" is well-established in the sense of a part. Since all paths have been developed and all defilements have been abandoned by an Arahant, they are not called "odhi." It should be understood that this definition "pahānā" (abandoning) is stated by way of the synonym for destroying (bhedana) [the defilements].
178:
By the word beginning with "sekha," the meaning expressed by the word *bhikkhu* is shown by way of virtue (*guṇa*). Below, however, it is shown by way of designation (*samaññā*) and profession (*paṭiññā*), and by way of etymological definition (*nibbacana*) with the word beginning with "bhikkhati."

By the words "sekho bhikkhu," the seven types of trainees (*sekha*) are spoken of. By the words "bhinnattā pāpakānaṃ...pe... bhikkhu," only the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is spoken of. These two do not agree with the [other] two: "by the word *sekha*, the seven noble ones along with the virtuous worldling (*kalyāṇa-puthujjana*); and by the word *bhinnattā*, the four established in the fruit (*phalaṭṭha*)." It should be understood that this disagreement is a direct (*nippariyāya*) presentation, not a figurative one. It was said, "In other places, the virtuous worldling and so forth are spoken of." Is it not also spoken of one who is a *bhikkhu* by profession (*paṭiññā*)? It is spoken of; however, here, because only a *bhikkhu* capable of producing all types of jhāna is intended, that [other] person is not intended.

The word of the Blessed One is called "ṭhāna" (ground/basis) because it is the cause for performing the act of higher ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*). That which is suitable for that word is called "ṭhānāraha." It means a formal act (*kammavācā*) with an undiminished motion (*ñatti*) and which is not recited out of order.

It means that it is virtue (*sīla*) in the primary sense because it is abstinence by undertaking (*samādāna-virati*) and abstinence by non-transgression (*avītikkamana-virati*). Referring to non-covetousness (*anabhijjhā*) and so forth, the figurative nature of mental virtue (*cetasika-sīla*) is mentioned. They say a city-builder is a master of the science of building sites (*vatthuvijjā-cariya*). The four types of nutriment are *asita* (eaten food) and so forth; or they are food to be chewed, eaten, licked, or sucked.

One endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha has closed faculties, because the three types of good conduct have the restraint of the faculties as their nutriment. Or, the restraint of the Pātimokkha is a strong dependence (*upanissaya*) for the restraint of the faculties. Thus, one whose faculties are closed by the restraint of the Pātimokkha is called "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuta*). With this intention, the meaning of the word "saṃvuta" is given as "one with closed faculties." It should be understood that the phrase "by the Pātimokkha and by restraint" is said with the intention that virtue other than the Pātimokkha is included by the mention of bodily non-transgression and so forth. The second meaning is stated referring to the identical meaning of both terms.

Intending that even covetousness and so forth are included by the phrase "all immorality" (*sabbampi dussīlyaṃ*), it is said, "he practices even with the mind; therefore, to show that." "Therein" refers to the improper conducts (*anācāra*) spoken of by way of bodily transgression and so forth. "He incurs the disposal of heavy articles" means he incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave) offense.
179:
"Āropima" refers to bamboo that has grown spontaneously on the Saṅgha's land. "Phātikamma" is the act of making something other than a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*) become a heavy article. By the Pali term "daṇḍakamma," the previously mentioned manual labor is meant. Because they bathe with powders such as siris-bark powder, that substance is called "sināna" (bath powder, etc., which is the cause of bathing).

One who habitually speaks pleasant words, whether true or false, is called "cāṭu" (a flatterer). The desire to be a speaker of pleasant words is called "cāṭukāma," and that state is called "cāṭukamyatā" (flattery). It means there is no place where mung bean soup cannot enter, as it is not incompatible with any food. This is the opinion of the commentator. He is called "paribhaṭa" because he carries/supports or because he nourishes. Or, a servant (*sevaka*) who is an attendant is called "paribhaṭa."

"Bhaṇḍāgārikakamma" refers to the work of a storekeeper performed for laypeople. Giving food first in order to receive food is called "piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍa." Or, accepting food offered in return after giving one's own food is called "piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍa." Managing the requisites of the Saṅgha and the requisites of the Cetiya in an improper way, or misusing items meant for the Saṅgha and Cetiya, or treating them as one's own property, as some teachers say.

It is called "gocara" (pasture/resort) because cattle graze in this place. It is called "gocara" because it is like a grazing ground for cattle. It is a place that should be frequented constantly. Or, "cattle" refers to the faculties such as the eye. The objects such as forms, which are the range of those faculties, are called "gocara." Since an unsuitable resort is called "agocara," a suitable resort other than that is called "gocara."

Because the word "vā" also has the meaning of shaking off (removing), he said "viniddhutakibbisāni vā."

They are called "oramattaka" (trifling/minor) because they have a limit that is the least of these faults. Faults that should be remedied or removed merely by restraint of body and speech are called "saṃyamakaraṇīya." Acts to be performed merely by mental restraint, such as "I will not do this again," or by the restraint of the faculties, are called "saṃvarakaraṇīya." One who habitually lives in the Divivihāra district is called "divivihāravāsī." The mental determination itself is called "adhiṭṭhānāvikamma." Here, the confession (*desanā*) is intended by "vuṭṭhānāvikamma." Therein, according to the teaching "to be performed by the arising of thought, connected with attention," it refers to faults that should not be transgressed and do not lead to an offense, for the sake of purifying the restraint of the Pātimokkha; this is the teacher's intention.

"Catubbidhassa" refers to the four fears: the fear of self-reproach, the fear of reproach by others, the fear of punishment, and the fear of an unhappy destination.

Intending that only a monk is meant by the text "idha bhikkhu," he said, "As for the remaining trainings, they are mentioned to show the meaning of the word *sikkhā* by way of extracting the meaning."
180:
The inclusion of the term 'bhikkhu' is done for the purpose of showing all four assemblies capable of producing all jhānas, by placing the foremost assembly at the head. Alternatively, because a monk is intended by way of virtue, it should be understood that all training (sikkhā) is intended here.

In the phrase 'sabbena sikkhāsamaādānena' (by the undertaking of all training), it refers to that undertaking by which all training rules are undertaken. Even if it is a single undertaking, it is called 'sabbasamādāna' (undertaking of all) because it performs the function of undertaking all training. In the case of multiple undertakings, there is no need to even mention it. 'Sabbena sikkhitabbākārena' (by every mode of training) refers to modes such as non-transgression, confession of offenses, rehabilitation from offenses, and the practice of duties. With reference to making the remaining training rules complete without exception through the power of non-transgression, the words 'bhinnassapi' and so forth are spoken.

Considering that meditation which purifies the mind from the obstructing hindrances (nīvaraṇa) is the devotion to wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga), the word 'bhāvanaṃ' (meditation) is spoken. 'Suppapariggāhakaṃ' refers to the clear comprehension (sampajañña) that distinguishes and grasps, thinking: 'This sleep does not exist before or after this (cognitive process); this (fatigue) is the cause of this sleep,' and so forth.

520-521. 'Yutto' means exerting effort. It shows the connection that one is devoted to wakefulness while maintaining continuous effort (sātacca) and mature wisdom (nepakka).

Regarding the phrase 'lokiyāyapi... āha', it means that in the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā), states such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) do not occur together on a single object. Even when they do occur, the faculties (indriya) and powers (bala) that arise are included only within the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga). This is because it is said, 'Joy (pāmojja) has faith as its strong supporting cause' (S.ii.23); thus, by taking the enlightenment factor of rapture (pīti-sambojjhaṅga), the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) and the power of faith (saddhā-bala), which are its strong supporting causes, are also taken. It should be understood that this is said with reference to the fact that only five path factors occur at the moment of insight.

Knowing the purposeful (sātthaka) and so forth in every mode, or rightly, or evenly, is 'sampajāna'; that itself is 'sampajañña' (clear comprehension). By that (sampajañña), because of its association with mindfulness, although mindfulness is not mentioned in the brief exposition (uddesa), it is intended to be spoken of by the word 'sato' in the detailed exposition (niddesa).

Knowing the purposeful nature of advancing and so forth is 'sātthaka-sampajañña' (clear comprehension of purpose). Likewise, there is 'sappāya-sampajañña' (clear comprehension of suitability). In the matters of advancing and so forth, whether at the place of alms-round or elsewhere, knowing without abandoning the resort (gocara) known as the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is 'gocara-sampajañña' (clear comprehension of the resort). Non-delusion in advancing and so forth is itself 'asammoha-sampajañña' (clear comprehension of non-delusion).
181:
The 'two kinds of speech' refer to speech regarding following instructions and not following instructions, which were not mentioned before. It means one only follows the instructions; because of being easy to admonish (suvaca), one gives a reply (speaks back).

'By the head of the meditation subject' (kammaṭṭhāna-sīsena) means by the excellence of the meditation subject, making the meditation subject the priority. By that phrase, it shows the meaning of going to the shrine without abandoning the meditation subject that will be mentioned in the passage 'the bowl is also insentient' and so forth, or the meditation subject that is currently being maintained. The word 'tasmā' (therefore) connects with the sentence 'dhammakathā kathetabbāyevāti vadanti' (they say that a Dhamma talk should indeed be given). 'Bhaye' refers to times of danger, such as the power of other kings.

'Avasesaṭṭhāne' refers to the place after the gruel has been taken. The mention of standing and walking is said by way of the postures that should be determined, not by way of rejecting sitting which must definitely be done at times such as eating.

The Elder Dārucīriya—
'Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: In the seen, there will be only the seen; in the heard, the sensed, and the cognized, there will be only the heard, the sensed, and the cognized. When, Bāhiya, for you, in the seen there is only the seen, and in the heard, the sensed, and the cognized there is only the heard, the sensed, and the cognized, then, Bāhiya, you will not be "with that." When, Bāhiya, you are not "with that," then, Bāhiya, you will not be "in that." When, Bāhiya, you are not "in that," then, Bāhiya, you will be neither here nor beyond nor in between the two. This itself is the end of suffering.' (Ud. 10)—
With just this much Dhamma, he realized the fruit of Arahantship.

Moving to the side to avoid a stump and so forth, or to avoid the foot that is planted, is called 'vītiharaṇa'. Alternatively, bringing the back foot up to the planted foot is 'atiharaṇa', and bringing it beyond that is 'vītiharaṇa'. This is the distinction between atiharaṇa and vītiharaṇa. 'Avīci' means without interval.

Regarding the phrase 'even in the first impulsion (javana)... does not occur', this is said with reference to the absence of lust and so forth for 'woman' or 'man' in the five-sense-door cognitive process (pañcavijñāṇavīthi). For in that process, through the power of unwise adverting and determining (ayoniso āvajjana-votthabbana), lust arises for a pleasant female form and so forth, and aversion arises for an unpleasant one. However, in the mind-door (manodvāra), lust and so forth for 'woman' or 'man' do occur.
182: The root of that mind-door impulsion (manodvārajavana) is the five-door impulsion (pañcadvārajavana), or all the consciousness starting from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as previously mentioned. Thus, the primary knowledge (mūlapariññā) is stated by fully understanding the life-continuum, which is the root of mind-door impulsion. Adventitiousness (āgantukatā) and temporariness (tāvakālikatā), however, occur by virtue of the five-door impulsion not having occurred before and lasting only for a moment. It is said that the Maṇisappa (gem-snake) is a species of snake found on the island of Ceylon (Sīhaḷadīpa). Calana means vibration. Atiharati means bringing up to the mouth. Vītiharati means bringing from the mouth to the stomach, or bringing food that has reached the stomach to the side. Allattañca anupāleti means protecting it so that it does not become excessively dry due to wind and so forth. Ābujati means reflecting on or knowing the searching for food, swallowing, digestion, and indigestion, etc. The effort (payoga) that accomplishes this knowing is called 'right effort' (sammāpayoga). Alternatively, knowing that 'relying on the right practice, there is no such person as a 'self' (attā) who is the consumer within' is called ābujana (reflection). Aṭṭhāne refers to unsuitable places occupied by humans or non-humans, such as fields, shrines, and so forth. Tumbato means from a water vessel such as a bamboo tube. Taṃ refers to discarded water. Gate means in the act of going. Since the bringing of the body forward and backward in going was already mentioned by the inclusion of abhikkama (advancing) and paṭikkama (receding), it should be understood that here only the act of going itself is taken. Or, the following meaning is the distinction between these words. Ettakena means that the clear comprehension of the resort (gocarasampajañña) is not yet evident merely by mentioning the maintenance of the four postures without abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Thus, just as the meditation subject is not evident during sleep, for one who discerns the phenomena occurring in walking, standing, and sitting, the phenomena occurring during sleep are not evident. Impulsion (javana) is called 'functional process' (kiriyāmayapavatta) because it causes bodily and other actions, and because it arises due to functional advertence (āvajjana-kiriyā). Or, all thought-processes (vīthicitta) occurring in the six doors are called functional processes. The second jhāna is called 'tuṇhībhāva' (silence) because it is devoid of verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhāra), namely vitakka and vicāra. Upāsanatthāna means the place for practicing and exerting in the meditation subject, like the place where archers practice their archery. To show that very meaning, it is called 'yogapatha' (the path of practice). Sīsaṃ dhovati (washing the head) signifies reaching the state of a free man after being liberated from the slavery of evil desires. Or, it is the washing away of the dust of ill-repute cast by those who practice wrongly.
183: According to the Vinaya method, it appears in the Pārājika on taking what is not given (adinnādāna). According to the Suttanta method, it appears in the Āraññaka training rule referring to a forest-dwelling monk, as 'pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchimaṃ' (at most five hundred bow-lengths). This is because that monk is described in the Suttas as 'āraññako pantasenāsano' (a forest-dweller in a remote lodging) due to living in the forest according to the Vinaya method. The place called 'nitumba' or 'nadīkuñja' is known as 'kandara' (a grotto or cleft). It is shown that even in non-mountainous regions, a place where river water recedes and is difficult to traverse is called a 'kandara'. By the phrase 'bhājetvā dassitaṃ' (shown by classification), the reason for the necessity of detailed classification and for providing the detailed explanation at the end is shown. An action performed in a secluded place is called 'rahassa'; that which is suitable or fit for that action is called 'rāhasseyyaka'. This is because Taddhita suffixes are diverse. Alternatively, a good action in seclusion is called 'rahassa', and that which is fit for it is 'rāhasseyyaka'. Paṇihita means well-placed (well-established). Pariggahitaniyyānaṃ means having the nature of deliverance through the grasping of the body and so forth. It means being endowed with the nature of deliverance due to the proper occurrence in objects such as the body. Alternatively, the knowledge that grasps the body and so forth is called 'pariggaha'; because of being associated with that knowledge, it means having established mindfulness which is grasped and is a means of deliverance. 542-543. 'Vikārappattiyā' means by way of the state of the mind reaching alteration. 'Sabbasaṅgāhikavasena' means by way of including all anger occurring towards beings and formations. It should be understood that the inclusion of all is done because the abandonment by eradication (samucchedappahāna) is intended. 'Idaṃ sandhāya' (referring to this) refers to the words 'dve dhammā' (two qualities). Although 'thinamiddha' (sloth and torpor) is indicated in the singular, in the detailed explanation (niddesa), the plural 'santā' is used, thus making a difference in number. The phrase 'nirodhasantatāya' (by the peacefulness of cessation) is used to exclude the peacefulness of the factors (aṅgasantatāya) or the peacefulness of nature (sabhāvasantatāya). The perception that is the opposite of sloth and torpor, being free from the alteration of sloth and torpor, is called 'ālokasaññā' (perception of light). Therefore, it is said, 'This perception is luminous'. Terms such as 'vantattā muttattā' and 'ālokā hoti' are called 'cattattā', etc. Or, by the word 'ādi' (and so forth), both...
184:
Collecting the terms of the description (niddesa), among those terms, whichever are synonyms (vevacana) of each other, it should be understood that it is said "they are synonyms of each other" with reference to those terms. By the word "paṭimuñcato", he shows the overcoming (abhibhava) accompanied by exertion (sārambha). Because of attending (ābhujati) and knowing (sampajānāti) without hindrance (nirāvaraṇa), it is called "nirāvaraṇābhoga". Because it has the nature of attending without hindrance, it is called "open" (vivaṭa).

It should be understood that remorse (vippaṭisāra) based on the transgression of an object (vatthujjhācāra) due to indecision such as "Is it past noon or not?" is called by the term "transgression of an object" (vatthujjhācāra) as a causal designation.

Regarding the word "kilissanti", they say it means "they defile" (kilesenti). Or, they themselves are defiled by the nature of distress (sadaratha). This is because when those hindrances (nīvaraṇa) arise, they do not arise free from defilement.

In this very Vibhaṅga, the word "upeto hoti" and so on have already been taught in the sections on the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkhasaṃvara) and so forth.

"By way of description" (niddesavasena) means they say it is by way of description (niddesa) such as "Among those, what is equanimity? That which is equanimity..." and by way of re-description (paṭiniddesa) such as "He is endowed with this equanimity." By this description, "Among those, what is... he is endowed with this equanimity," the person (puggala) is indicated. By the re-description "samupeto" and so on, he is indicated again. Or, the person is indicated up to the word "samannāgato". By this re-description, "Therefore he is called upekkhako," the person is indicated again. In this way, the description and re-description should be connected by way of those words. "By way of variety" (pakārena) means they establish the meaning of the word "upekkhako" by way of the variety of the Dhamma such as "upekkhana" (the act of looking on) and by way of the variety of the person such as "upeto samupeto". The meaning "upekkhana" is the cause for the meaning "upekkhā". This is because the meaning "upekkhā" exists by way of looking on (upekkhana). Similarly, the meaning "upāgato samupāgato" is the cause for the meanings "upeto samupeto". In this way, desiring to show the cause of each meaning by way of the Dhamma and the person, they explain it. Or, they explain it by showing the cause for the meaning of "upekkhako" itself by way of "He is endowed with this equanimity" and so on. They analyze by showing the variety of syllables (byañjana) such as "upekkhana, ajjhupekkhana, samupeto". Or, the separate explanation of the meaning of "upekkhā" included within the word "upekkhako" and the word "upekkhako" itself is given as "That which is equanimity is called upekkhana" and so on, and "He is endowed with this equanimity" and so on...
185:
This is the analysis of syllables (byañjanavibhāga). The state of being overturned so as not to be known in every way is called "aññātatā" (unknownness). Even if known in some way, the state of not being able to be delimited without remainder is called "gambhīrabhāva" (profundity).

This phrase "uparibhūmippattiyā" should be applied only to this place: "rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā" (surpassing perceptions of form). Or, since the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) etc. are also higher planes (uparibhūmi) than the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāsānañcāyatana) etc., it is not illogical in all places; it is indeed appropriate.

In the description of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana-niddesa), in the Pali passage "anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ" and so on, "tena vuccati anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ", the word "viññāṇena" is an instrumental case (karaṇavacana) used in the sense of the accusative case. It is said in the Commentary that one attends to the consciousness that pervades that very space-concept. Or, the meaning of this Pali is: one attends to the consciousness pervading that space-concept with the Viññāṇañcāyatana-consciousness. However, only this meaning is appropriate: having pervaded that space-concept with consciousness, one attends to it according to the mode grasped by that consciousness; thus, that consciousness pervades infinitely. This is because it is said that one who possesses the first immaterial consciousness pervades the space-concept infinitely with consciousness, and one who possesses the second immaterial consciousness attends to that consciousness together with its mode of pervading and pervades infinitely.

"Taṃyeva viññāṇaṃ abhāveti" means (not producing) that very consciousness which was previously attended to as "infinite consciousness". This is because just as one does not produce the sign of form (rūpanimitta) through the first jhāna, one no longer produces the first immaterial consciousness, which is the object of that second immaterial consciousness, through the third immaterial attainment.

## The Explanation of the Description is finished.

## The Explanation of the Suttanta Classification is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification

In showing the fivefold method (pañcakanaya) in the Abhidhamma Classification, it is extracted by Pali such as "five jhānas" and "therein, what is the first jhāna?". It is because of showing the four jhānas—first, third, fourth, and fifth—already extracted in the fourfold method, and because of showing the distinction of the second jhāna alone.

## The Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification is finished.
186:
## 3. Commentary on the Questionnaire

Regarding these supramundane states, among these three jhanas, the statement "supramundane states having the immeasurable as object may arise" means that these jhanas, categorized in this way, are indeed supramundane at the time of the Path or the Fruit. The fourth jhanas of the limited-space kasina, the light kasina, mindfulness of breathing, and the divine abidings should be understood as being included in the fourth jhana that serves as the basis for all (sabbattha-pādaka).

The statement that the Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants "have developed the Path and realized the Fruit" or "will develop and will realize" should be understood as being spoken by way of the lower Paths and Fruits. This discussion occurs regarding the thirteen fourth jhanas arising from the wholesome (kusala). One cannot see the Path and Fruit of Arahantship through the wholesome fourth jhana.

In the phrase "among the thirteen arising from the functional (kiriya)," since there is no functional supramundane fourth jhana, it should be said "among the twelve." Alternatively, it should be understood that among the thirteen arising from the wholesome, the fourth jhana of the Fruit of the trainee (sekkha) is included, and it is spoken of as "among the thirteen arising from the functional" together with the fourth jhana of the non-trainee (asekkha). Here, whatever higher knowledges (abhiññā) and so forth the Arahants possess, because it is the basis for all those higher knowledges, it is known as "basis for all" (sabbattha-pādaka). This is because for those Arahants, there is no further round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Or, it should be understood as "basis for all" because it is similar to the basis for all in being indescribable, like the fourth jhana of the limited-space kasina and so forth.

Mental formation (manosaṅkhāra) refers to perception and feeling, or else the four aggregates. In the phrase "starting with the sign" (nimittaṃ ārabbha), it should be said "the sign and Nibbāna."

In the Paṭṭhāna Pali text, "A state internal to oneself is a condition for a state internal to oneself by way of object-condition," it is taught that "Internal aggregates are a condition for the reflection of the knowledge of the various psychic powers, the knowledge of recollection of past lives, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma, and the knowledge of the future by way of object-condition." Therefore, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa) does not only know the kamma in the continuity of others like the knowledge of penetrating the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa); rather, just as the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) makes manifest unmanifest matter, it also makes manifest unmanifest kamma in one's own continuity. Therefore, it is said "at the time of knowing one's own kamma."

## The Commentary on the Questionnaire is finished.
## The Commentary on the Analysis of the Jhanas is finished.
187:
## 13. Analysis of the Immeasurables
## 1. Commentary on the Suttanta Classification

By the word "sabbadhī" (everywhere), the pervasion without limit in terms of the boundary of directions and regions is taught. By the phrase "sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ" (to all as to oneself, the entire world), pervasion in terms of the limit of beings is taught. Therefore, it is said "for the purpose of showing the absence of limits." The reason the word "tathā" or "iti" is not spoken is because that pair, which could follow the phrase "with a mind imbued with loving-kindness," is not the basis for the various ways of pervading loving-kindness and so forth; thus, it is not spoken, and it means that "with a mind imbued with loving-kindness" is stated again.

Loving-kindness protected by shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) does not decline, because it does not reach the failure (vipatti) of lust (rāga) and affection (sineha), which are like near enemies.

"Adhimuñcitvā" means having pervaded well. To show that well-pervading, "adhikabhāvena" (by way of excellence) and so forth are said. Or, it means having resolved firmly with strong resolution (adhimokkha).

"Heṭṭhā vultoyeva" (as said below) means that the meaning of the terms "sabbena sabbaṃ, sabbathā sabbaṃ" was taught in the Analysis of the Jhanas (Jhānavibhaṅga) as "all training with all undertaking of training, all training by way of all modes of training." However, in this Analysis of the Immeasurables, it is appropriate to take the meaning as "the entire world of beings by way of all limits, by way of equality with oneself, and by way of association with all beings; the entire world by way of the modes of pervading all limited directions and so forth."

"Paccatthika-vighāta-vasena" means by way of destroying the near and far enemies of loving-kindness and so forth, such as lust (rāga) and ill-will (byāpāda). Whichever immeasurable is without limit, that immeasurable is the cause for the arising of a mind without enmity; this is another way the meaning of that text can be stated.

Hell and so forth are called destiny (gati). Castes such as the Caṇḍāla are called family (kula). The non-obtaining of alms-food and so forth is called wealth (bhoga). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), ugliness and so forth should be included.

## The Commentary on the Suttanta Classification is finished.
188:
## 3. Commentary on the Questionnaire

By this statement, "In this text... it is taught," the mundane nature of the immeasurables taught in this Analysis of the Immeasurables (Appamaññāvibhaṅga) is shown, distinguishing them from the Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandhavibhaṅga) and so forth. Therefore, it is not the case that the teaching of supramundane immeasurables in other Analyses (Vibhaṅgas) is permitted.

## The Commentary on the Questionnaire is finished.

## The Commentary on the Analysis of the Immeasurables is finished.
