## 14. Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga
## 1. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā
'Patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena' means in the sense of being a foundation, either by way of association (sampayoga) or by way of decisive support (upanissaya), acting as a location (okāsa).

Liquor produced by mixing and kneading various ingredients such as flour, cakes, cooked rice, and yeast is called 'surā'. The juice of various ingredients such as flowers like the Madhuka, fruits like the jackfruit, sugarcane, and grapes, which has been fermented for a long time, is called 'meraya', meaning alcohol (āsava).

'Taṃsampayuttattā' means because of being associated with abstinence (virati), or because of being associated with the volition of abstinence (viraticetanā).

'Kammapathā eva' means that among the groups such as jhāna, which are not common to all states, it is included in the group of the courses of action (kammapatha). Regarding the drinking of intoxicants (surāpāna), it is said (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya) that "Monks, the practice of drinking intoxicants... leads to hell," thus appearing as a separate course of action. If this were so, there would be eleven courses of action; therefore, it should be understood that this drinking of intoxicants is included within the aforementioned ten courses of action by way of its supportive nature and similarity.

The state of having beings, women, and men as objects should be understood as having formations (saṅkhāra) as objects taken in that manner. For has it not been said, "The five training rules have limited objects (sensual objects)"? And it will be said (in the Commentary), "All these training rules, having the thing to be transgressed as an object, abstain from them through the volitions of enmity (vera-cetanā)."

'Gorūpasīlaka' refers to one who is naturally good. The phrase "for the sake of even a kākaṇika (a small coin)" etc., is said in the context of speaking falsehood driven by greed. In the context of speaking falsehood driven by hatred, the ultimate case of causing a schism in the Saṅgha is taken. In speaking falsehood driven by hatred for the purpose of another's ruin, the degree of being slightly blameworthy or greatly blameworthy should be applied according to the virtues of the person concerned and according to the intensity of the desire for ruin. Since the efforts (payoga) such as nissaggiya (throwing away), thāvara (permanent), vijjāmaya (by science/magic), and iddhimaya (by psychic power) are included only within the efforts of sāhatthika (by one's own hand) and āṇattika (by command), only these two are taken.

The statement "All five are indeed courses of action" is said with reference to figurative virtue (pariyāyasīla) known as volition (cetanā). Abstinence-virtue (viratisīla), however, belongs to the group of the Path factors. "Tesaṃ pana" means in the transgression of the remaining virtues.

It was stated as 'koṭṭhāsabhāvena' (by way of being a portion), but it should rather be stated as 'patiṭṭhānabhāvena' (by way of being a foundation). In this section on the training rules (sikkhāpadavāra), for an Arahant who has abandoned the five impossible states (abhabbaṭṭhāna), since enmity (vera) to be abstained from is entirely absent, there are no abstinences (virati) in functional (kiriya) consciousness; therefore, they are not extracted and taught. For trainees (sekha), although the five enmities have been abandoned, because unwholesome states and the roots of enmity such as greed, which are similar to those enmities, still exist, the arising of abstinences is not non-existent (it indeed occurs).

Bodily actions and so forth originating from the unwholesome are indeed enmities such as bodily misconduct in the continuity of those trainees. The abstinences of those trainees from those enmities are indeed possible.
190:
Since the enmities to be abstained from are entirely absent, there are no abstinences (virati) in functional (kiriya) consciousness, and thus they are not extracted and shown (in the text). For trainees (sekha), although the five enmities have been abandoned, because unwholesome states such as greed, which are similar to those enmities and are the roots of enmity, still exist, the arising of abstinences is not non-existent (it indeed occurs). Bodily actions and so forth originating from the unwholesome are indeed enmities such as bodily misconduct for those trainees; abstinences from those enmities do indeed arise. For that very reason, the three higher paths, which are not the fruit, possess the eight factors. In the section on training (sikkhāvāra), since they are not states to be developed (abhāvetabba), the states of the fruit (phala) are also not states to be trained (asikkhitabba). The functional states (kiriya) arising in the continuity of a person who has completed the training (an Arahant) are also not states to be trained. Therefore, some indeterminate (abyākata) states are not extracted and shown as training (sikkhā).

## The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Classification is finished.

## 2. Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā

"Sampattavirativasena" means by way of abstaining from what should be abstained from when a present object is encountered.

## The Commentary on the Catechism is finished.

## The Commentary on the Analysis of the Training Rules is finished.
191:
## 15. Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga
## 1. Suttantabhājanīya
## 1. Saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā
Having shown briefly, "This is the method," the teacher says "Dhammapabhedassa hi" and so forth to show that same method in detail. The divisions of Nirutti (Language) and Paṭibhāna (Perspicacity) should be understood by dividing their objects, such as Attha (Meaning/Result) and so forth, through divisions such as the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna) and so forth.

By this Pali phrase, "Whatever is conditionally arisen" (yaṃ kiñci paccayasamuppannaṃ), the teacher has included the results such as suffering (dukkha) that appear in the sections on the Truths (Sacca), Causes (Hetu), States (Dhamma), and Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda). Five types of Attha should be understood by way of what is stated in the Pali: Nibbāna in the sections on the Truths and Dependent Origination; the meaning taught in the section on the Scriptural Study (Pariyatti); and the resultant (vipāka) and functional (kiriya) in the Abhidhamma classification (Abhidhammabhājanīya). The same applies to the Dhammas.

The definition "Vidahati" (it arranges/produces) is a general definition common to causes that produce results (nibbattakahetu) and so forth. To clarify its meaning, the teacher says, "It sets in motion (pavatteti) and it leads to (pāpeti)." Among those, the former meaning of 'setting in motion' (pavattana) should be seen in states other than the Path (magga). For even the taught word is to be understood as setting the meaning in motion by way of making it known. However, since the Path leads to Nibbāna, the latter meaning of 'leading to' (pāpana) should be seen in that Path.

In the phrase "dhammaniruttābhilāpe," considering that the word 'Dhamma' expresses 'nature' (sabhāva), the teacher says, "Ya sabhāvanirutti" (which is the natural expression); the meaning is the expression that is spoken truly and without perversion. Some teachers explain that knowledge occurs in the utterance of the designation (paññatti), which is a collective sound and not the ultimate sound (paramattha sadda) that is uttered. If this were so, the fault would arise that only the collective designation should be uttered, and the individual ultimate sound should not be uttered. In fact, there is no other utterable sound apart from the ultimate sound. If it were the case that the meaning to be known through collective sounds like 'phassa' (contact) should be uttered, then, since there is no meaning to be known through those collective sounds apart from Attha and Dhamma, they would end up being Nirutti. It has already been shown that the masculine word 'Phasso' is a natural expression (sabhāvanirutti), while the neuter 'Phassaṃ' and feminine 'Phassā' are not natural expressions. There is no such thing as an utterance that is not an ultimate sound; therefore, the meaning should be understood as: knowledge in the utterance of that natural expression, which is itself a vocal sound, is called Nirutti-paṭisambhidā.

Because it is said that the knowledge that has reached the division in the utterance of that natural expression for one who reviews it, making that natural expression sound as the object, is Nirutti-paṭisambhidā, they say that the Nirutti-paṭisambhidā knowledge occurs in the mind-door following the ear-consciousness process (sotaviññāṇavīthi) which has the uttered sound as its object.
192:
They say that the knowledge of the Discrimination of Language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā) arises. The statement "The Discrimination of Language has a present object" is said with reference to knowing afterwards, having taken the sound which is the word. If this were the case, it would result in saying that another present object is [actually] another present object (an object of the past).

For example, just as the knowledge of the divine ear (dibbasota) is the cause for deciding the distinctions of sounds of humans, non-humans, etc., and clarifies those various sounds, so too, if the knowledge that has the present natural expression as its object and clarifies that sound—being the cause for deciding between natural expression (sabhāvanirutti) and non-natural expression—is called the Discrimination of Language, there is no contradiction with the Pali. It cannot be said that it does not produce the reflecting knowledge having the present sound as its object for one who reflects by taking that natural expression as an object; indeed, it can be said. That knowledge, while clarifying the natural expression, arises immediately after reflecting on those various sounds as the cause for deciding those various distinctions, thus distinguishing and penetrating the expression; therefore, it is also a knowledge that has reached distinction.

"Natural expression" (sabhāvanirutti) refers to the Magadhi (Māgadhī) language. Therefore, with reference to sounds other than Magadhi, such as Sanskrit (Sakkaṭa), the [commentator] said "But another..." "Byañjana" refers to particles (nipāta).

It has been stated in the ancient commentaries. The word "Bodhimanda" should be understood only as the place where the Four Noble Truths were first penetrated, not in every place where a Bodhi tree stands. "Suvaṇṇasalāka" means a noble voting ticket; it means taking a ticket for the purpose of preaching the Dhamma. It is not an invitation made while established in the knowledge of Discrimination (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, because it is to be known by a method other than the knowledge of Discrimination, the knowledge of the Sanskrit language is not the function of the Discrimination of Language.

This matter has been stated now to make known the status of the Magadhi language as the natural expression. Even among animals, such as in the Chaddanta Elephant King Jātaka, the Magadhi language is prevalent; the Oṭṭaka language or Sanskrit is not prevalent.

Among those languages, the other languages besides Magadhi certainly change and perish over time. Magadhi, however, though it may change in some places and at some times, does not change in all places, at all times, and in all ways. Because it remains even at the destruction of the world-cycle (kappavināsa), it is said: "This Magadhi alone does not change." "Papañca" means occurring for a long time. Only the word of the Buddha is the object of this knowledge. That is why Citta the householder, when asked about the verse beginning with "Nelaṅgo setapacchādo," asked: "Venerable Sir, was this spoken by the Blessed One?" When answered, "Yes, householder," he said: "Venerable Sir, then wait a moment while I reflect on its meaning with my knowledge."
193:
Sabbatthaka-ñāṇa is the knowledge regarding meanings (attha) and so forth. This knowledge is called "Sabbatthaka-ñāṇa" because it occurs in those three (attha, dhamma, nirutti), or because it occurs in all four (attha, dhamma, nirutti, paṭibhāna), or because it occurs only in the three due to being the meaning of the state (dhammattha) of the analytical knowledge of perspicacity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā), which is of the nature of wholesome functional [consciousness]. It is called Sabbatthaka because the knowledges that are accompanied by meaning should be reflected upon as "These knowledges illuminate this meaning," or because this knowledge has all meanings such as attha and dhamma as its object. Alternatively, it is called Sabbatthaka because it is cast into (takes as object) all objects. It is said that the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) occurring at the stage of a learner (sekha) become clear upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship. However, just like previous effort (pubbayoga), the attainment of Arahantship is not not a cause (i.e., it is indeed a cause) for the clarity of an Arahant's analytical knowledge. Therefore, the fact that the five causes are the reasons for the clarity of the analytical knowledge of both learners (sekha) and non-learners (asekha) should be applied accordingly.

The commentary is called "Paripucchā" (Inquiry) because it is the discourse that occurs after a question. In the phrase "they will consider that the practice (paṭipatti) should be fulfilled," it means that by giving weight to practice and wishing to disparage material gain, one reflects, "Even a blanket worth a hundred thousand, I have cut and shredded with a small knife to make a fringe; those Dhamma-preachers who carry the scriptures (pariyatti) and give weight to gain will not consider becoming like me." Here also, by showing the lack of clarity in the Elder previously due to the occurrence of doubt, and by showing the clarity upon reaching Arahantship through the answering of the problem after reaching Arahantship, [the importance of attainment] is shown. It is said that the Elder Tissa mentioned here is the same Elder Tissa mentioned immediately before.

Differentiation (pabheda) is the reaching of distinction in the analytical knowledges attained through the paths. Attainment (adhigama) is the acquisition (paṭilābha) through those paths; therefore, that attainment should be understood as supramundane (lokuttara), while differentiation should be understood as belonging to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). "Na pana tathā" means that just as it is a strong condition for attainment, it is not such a strong condition for differentiation. Now, wishing to show that scriptural study (pariyatti) and so forth are not strong conditions for attainment, and that previous effort (pubbayoga) is a strong condition, he said "Pariyattisavanaparipucchā hi" and so forth. In that statement, "there is no analytical knowledge" means there is no attainment (adhigama) of analytical knowledge. Now, wishing to show the intended meaning, he said "Ime pana" and so forth. Since both previous effort and attainment are causes for clarity, it is said, "Previous effort is a strong condition for differentiation."

## The Explanation of the Summary Section (Sangahavāra) is finished.
194:
## 2. Explanation of the Section on Truths, etc.
In the Section on Causes (Hetuvāra), the group of states that are the results of causes in all three periods of time—past, future, and present—are called "attha". The causal states of those are called "dhamma". In the Section on States (Dhammavāra), however, because past states are included by the power of the veneyya (those to be guided), terms like "uppanna" (arisen) and "samuppanna" (thoroughly arisen) are not mentioned; instead, past and present results are called "attha", and the causal states that produce those results are called "dhamma". This is the distinction between these two sections.

## The Explanation of the Section on Truths, etc. is finished.
## The Explanation of the Suttanta Classification is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification
"Because it is not mentioned" means that after speaking generally as "knowledge in those resultants (vipāka)," it is not mentioned specifically. In this Abhidhamma classification method, because functional (kiriya) states do not have the nature of producing results, their status as "dhamma" (cause) is not mentioned.

If that is so, since functional states do not have resultant fruits, should their status as "attha" (result) also not be mentioned? No, [it should be mentioned] because they are conditioned states (paccayuppanna) produced by causes. If their status as "attha" is asserted because they are conditioned, then since wholesome (kusala) and unwholesome (akusala) states can also be conditioned, do they not also become "attha"? This is not prohibited. However, because they are prominent as the primary causes of results, only their status as "dhamma" is mentioned.

If it is asked, "Since functional states are conditions, do they not also become 'dhamma'?" This is not a fault, as it is not prohibited [that they are causes]. However, because functional states are not the cause of the state connected with the fruit of kamma, their status as "dhamma" is not mentioned.

Alternatively, for one who reflects on wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional states only by their nature (sabhāva), without making a distinction such as "this is the cause of this, this is the result produced by the cause," both Dhamma-paṭisambhidā and Attha-paṭisambhidā occur. For this reason also, it should be understood that their status as attha and dhamma is not mentioned [in the usual sequence].

In the sections on wholesome and unwholesome states, Dhamma-paṭisambhidā is able to see the causal status, the specific potency, and the result to be produced; thus, it looks toward the result to be produced. Therefore, in connection with that result to be produced, it is said, "Knowledge in those resultants is Attha-paṭisambhidā." The function of Attha-paṭisambhidā is merely seeing the nature, because it sees only the finished result. Since that Attha-paṭisambhidā does not look toward the producing cause, it should be understood that in the section on resultants, it is not said, "Knowledge in those ripening states is Dhamma-paṭisambhidā."

"By way of designation of nature (sabhāva-paññatti)" means not by way of designation of beings (satta) and so forth, but by way of unerring designation. "Having stirred up (khobhetvā)" means having stirred up by way of causing hair-raising, the shouting of "Sadhu," giving gifts, and so forth. Again...
195:
"You will know upon hearing the Dhamma" means that because of their limited learning, when he speaks for the second time, he will speak that very same Dhamma.

In the phrase "for the purpose of showing the planes (bhūmi)," the sense-sphere plane and the supramundane plane should be understood as "planes." Alternatively, the sense-sphere thought-arisings and the supramundane thought-arisings should also be understood as "planes."

## The Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Interrogation (Pañhapucchaka)

By the words "the meaning (attha) which is conditionally arisen, and the conditional phenomena (dhamma)," he shows the synonym of meaning (atthapariyāya) of the wholesome, unwholesome, and material phenomena arisen from causes such as root-causes (hetu), as well as the synonym of phenomena (dhammapariyāya) of the resultant, functional, and material phenomena that are the conditions such as root-causes. The state of having sense-sphere resultants as objects and the state of having sublime (mahaggata) states as objects for the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā) is not appropriate in the context of having the knowledge of analytical insights as objects. This is because the knowledges of analytical insights arise in sense-sphere wholesome and supramundane wholesome states, as well as in sense-sphere functional and supramundane resultant states. If it were to take all knowledge as its object, it would be appropriate. However, because of the statement, "By which knowledge one knows those knowledges" (Vibh. 726), they say it does not take all knowledge as its object. In the Suttanta Classification, however, since it is stated without distinction that "the knowledge of knowledges is the analytical insight of perspicuity," it should take all knowledge as its object. In the Abhidhamma Classification as well, since the teaching by way of the arising of consciousness is an exhaustive teaching, the statement "By which knowledge one knows those knowledges," spoken by way of the objects already shown, does not prohibit having other objects. Just as the objects of the analytical insight of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) are not exhaustively taught in the Abhidhamma Classification, so too the objects of the analytical insight of perspicuity are not exhaustively taught. Thus, because the analytical insight of perspicuity takes all knowledge as its object, it is stated: "Three analytical insights may have limited (paritta) objects, may have sublime (mahaggata) objects, or may have immeasurable (appamāṇa) objects" (Vibh. 749).

If, because of the statement "The analytical insight of meaning may not have the path as its object" (Vibh. 749), the method of interrogation (pañhapucchaka) proceeds only regarding the analytical insights taught in the Abhidhamma Classification. For the path is not something that is not conditionally arisen (i.e., it is conditionally arisen), and since in the Abhidhamma Classification, the analytical insight of perspicuity is taught as having only the knowledge of analytical insights as its object, it might be thought that its state of having sublime objects is not possible. Even so, these two Pali texts contradict each other. Among those texts, relying on the stronger Pali...
196:
Relying on the stronger Pali text, the intended meaning of the other Pali text should be sought. Furthermore, since the penetration of the conditionally arisen nature of wholesome and unwholesome states is not separate from the penetration of their nature as wholesome and unwholesome, the analytical insight of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā) regarding those wholesome and unwholesome states is direct (nippariyāya), because its object is definitely a phenomenon (dhamma). Similarly, since the penetration of the nature of resultants and functionals as conditions is not separate from the penetration of their nature as resultants and functionals, the analytical insight of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) regarding those resultants and functionals is direct (nippariyāya), because its object is definitely a meaning (attha).

Moreover, because it clarifies what should be known, there is no knowledge that is non-perspicuous (appaṭibhāna). Therefore, the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā) should directly (nippariyāya) apply to all knowledge. In the occurrence of the interrogation regarding the direct analytical insights, both Pali texts do not contradict each other.

In the phrase "having external objects because of having sound as an object," it should be "because of having the sound of another's speech as an object." This is because merely having sound as an object is not the cause for having an external object, since sound also exists internally (within oneself). It should be understood that the qualifier "of another's speech" was not made because that very sound follows the context.

## The Explanation of the Interrogation is finished.

## The Explanation of the Classification of Analytical Insights is finished.
197:
## 16. Classification of Knowledge (Ñāṇavibhaṅga)

## 1. Explanation of the Matrix of Ones, etc.

In the sense of being a location (okāsaṭṭhena), the phenomena associated with knowledge, as well as the object, are called the "basis" (vatthu) of knowledge. "Clarification of the basis as it really is" (yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā) means the clarification of a basis that has a single, unerring mode such as "non-root-cause" (na-hetu). Just as one instance of five-fold consciousness is a non-root-cause, so too another instance is a non-root-cause; the object of knowledge which is associated with such unerring commonality and is grasped by knowledge is called the "basis as it really is" (yāthāvakavatthu). Alternatively, the wisdom that clarifies the basis by way of unerring commonality as it really is, is called "clarification of the basis as it really is."

Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the dyads" (dukānurūpehi), they say it means "in accordance with the Matrix of Dyads." However, since the final dyad is taught without depending on the Matrix of Dyads, it should be said "in accordance with the nature of dyads." The same should be understood for the phrase "in accordance with the triads" (tikānurūpehi). In the final dyad, "meaning" (attha) refers to the fruit (phala). Since verbal roots have many meanings, it is called "producer of meaning" (atthajāpikā) because it produces that fruit; this is wisdom pertaining to the cause. It is called "that for which the meaning is produced" (jāpitatthā) because it has the fruit produced by this wisdom; this is wisdom associated with the fruit, which clarifies the fruit and is similar to the causal wisdom.

## 10. Explanation of the Matrix of Tens

By the words, "Sāriputta, there are these four modes of generation (yoni). Which four... he who knows me thus" (M. i. 152), the knowledge that distinguishes the four modes of generation is taught. By the words, "Sāriputta, I also know hell," etc. (M. i. 153), the knowledge that distinguishes the five destinations (gati) is taught. It is said, "In the Saṃyutta, seventy-three knowledges and seventy-seven knowledges are mentioned." Among them, in the Nidānavagga Saṃyutta, seventy-seven and forty-four knowledges are mentioned. As for the seventy-three knowledges, they are found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga starting with the knowledge based on learning (sutamaya), but not in the Saṃyutta. By the phrase "and other knowledges," it includes the knowledges taught here in this Vibhaṅga by way of the ones, etc.; the knowledges taught elsewhere such as "knowledge of the past" (pubbante ñāṇa), etc.; and the various types of knowledge taught in the Brahmajāla Sutta, etc., such as "This the Tathāgata knows: 'These grounds for views are thus grasped,'" and so forth. Because of the penetration of things as they really are, the knowledge itself is unshakable, and it makes the person endowed with that knowledge exceedingly powerful regarding the things to be known (ñeyya). Therefore, it is said, "in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of being a support (upatthambhaka)."
198:
The supreme state is Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). The Buddhas are called 'Āsabhā' (Supreme) either because they proceed towards Omniscient Knowledge by virtue of their declaration, or because they are approached by the eight assemblies. By the phrase 'Idaṃ pana,' it refers to Omniscient Knowledge itself as the station of the Buddhas. 'Tiṭṭhamāno vā' means that even if not speaking, merely by standing, it is considered a declaration. Regarding the eight assemblies, the Buddha roars a courageous roar, being endowed with the unshakable knowledge shown by the words: "Sāriputta, I know many hundreds of assemblies of Khattiyas... I do not see any reason why fear or hesitation would overcome me in those assemblies." (This is to be understood) through the Sīhanāda Sutta found in the Khandhaka Vaggas.

By the remainder of the sutta, "The four wheels (Catu-cakka) of devas and humans turn," it should be understood that the term 'cakka' (wheel) in that sutta refers to the sequential occurrence of the wheels of success, which are the results of causes such as relying on good people (sappurisu-passaya), or the continuous occurrence of subsequent wheels of success based on previous ones. Because the task of penetration is completed, the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship is called 'Paṭivedha' (Penetration), and it is said to "arise at the moment of the Fruit (Phala)." The completion of the function of the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa), which has the benefit of pointing out to others what has been attained through that penetration, occurs merely by the realization; thus it is said to "occur at the moment of the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) of Aññāsi Koṇḍañña." Thereafter, the occurrence of the knowledge of teaching until Parinibbāna should be understood as the station of that Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) which has been set in motion, just like the station of the wheel-treasure of a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) whose wheel has been set in motion.

They are called 'Samādānāni' because they are well-undertaken; regarding those undertakings, it is said "those performed after having undertaken them." Alternatively, by saying that kamma itself is 'Kamma-samādāna,' it shows that there is no new meaning in the word 'samādāna,' just as in the word 'muttagata,' the word 'gata' (has no separate meaning).

'Agatigāminī' refers to the practice leading to Nibbāna. For was it not taught: "Sāriputta, I know Nibbāna, and I know the practice leading to Nibbāna"?

'Hānabhāgiya-dhamma' refers to states that have the nature of decline, or states such as perceptions associated with sense-desire (kāma-sahagata-saññā). 'Taṃ kāraṇaṃ' refers to previously performed volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), and so forth.

This word 'Idāni' should be read in conjunction with the phrase "should be understood as having been taught in this sequence." By dividing the terms 'obstruction of defilements' (kilesāvaraṇa) and 'the absence of that,' it refers to the absence of the obstruction of defilements. For the attainment of the destruction of defilements, the obstruction of defilements is not the cause (aṭṭhāna), but only the absence of that obstruction is the cause (ṭhāna). For non-attainment, the obstruction of defilements is the cause, while the absence of that obstruction is not the cause.
199:
The absence of that (obstruction) is not the cause (aṭṭhāna). In that context, by taking the absence of that obstruction, the Buddha sees the existence of Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi) such as "there is that which is given," etc., and the absence of the cause for Wrong View (Micchādiṭṭhi) which is the opposite of that Right View. To establish this meaning—that the Blessed One, with this knowledge, sees the obstruction of defilements and its absence, which are the causes and non-causes for attainment and non-attainment—it is said: "Because of seeing the existence of mundane Right View and because of seeing the absence of the cause for fixed Wrong View (Niyata-micchādiṭṭhi)." Here, only the seeing of the cause for attainment is intended, because later, the seeing of the absence of the obstruction of result (vipākāvaraṇa) by power of the capable person (bhabba-puggala) will be discussed. However, it should be understood that other attainments and non-attainments are also mentioned here by implication, as they are accomplished by this knowledge. 'Because of seeing the diversity of elements' (Dhātu-vematta) means seeing the diversity of elements associated with lust (rāga), etc., by power of their intensity; or seeing the causes of temperament (cariya) such as "this person is of lustful temperament because this element is intense"; or it means seeing the diversity of elements like lust, etc., as lust and so forth are themselves elements by their intrinsic nature. 'Without taking effort' (Payogaṃ anādiyitvā) means preaching by power of liberation without regarding the effort associated with sensual lust or ill-will, as in the cases of the Minister Santati, Aṅgulimāla, and others.

## 1. Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā

In the phrase 'Na hetum eva,' the meaning is 'Na hetū eva' (they are not causes). For the sake of euphony (vyañjana-siliṭṭhatā), the vowel is shortened and the letter 'ma' is inserted, as in the word 'adukkhamasukhā.' In the phrase 'By this method also,' the distinction should be understood that the former method negates the state of being a cause, while the latter method includes the category of states that are not causes (na-hetu-dhamma).

By the word 'Cuti' (death), one should understand the taking of a single birth bounded by death. By the word 'Bhava' (existence), the existence taught in nine ways is taken. By the state of being included within those (destinies and existences), they are said to be 'included' in those respective places. By the phrase 'Only that which is cognizable by mind-consciousness as it arises,' the distinction of these (fivefold consciousnesses) from matter (rūpa) is made, as "matter is not like that which is cognizable by the six consciousnesses as it arises."

'Even passing from aeon to aeon, it does not arise' means it never arises in that manner (with different doors or objects). It shows that these fivefold consciousnesses do not have a diversity of characteristics different from what has been stated, unlike milk and other substances (which change into curd, etc.).

'Having combined' means having combined all matter existing in the world. By this, while showing the non-manifestation even in greatness, he cuts off the quibble that it would not be manifest due to subtlety.
200:
The pedantic argument that "it will not be made manifest" is cut off. "In my physical basis, which is the eye-sensitivity" is the meaning. "Visaya" is intended as the locus of sovereignty (domain).

"Abbokiṇṇā" means unobstructed, having no interval. It means that by this word "anantarā," the fixed sequence (paṭipāṭiniyama) of the five consciousnesses, which are distinct, is negated. "Anantaratā" means that the state of the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) is negated by this Pali. By the word "samanantaratā," the state of the contiguity condition (samanantara-paccaya) is also negated.

"Ābhujanato" means because of performing a turn, like a rotation, or because of causing to turn back. Here also, "the five consciousnesses are without advertence (anābhoga)" means they do not have the nature of advertence (ābhoga-sabhāva), which is like turning. In the Pali passages such as "the five consciousnesses have no adverting (āvaṭṭana)," the meaning should be understood as the absence of the function of adverting (āvaṭṭanabhāva).

In this Pali, "does not specifically cognize any phenomenon (dhamma)," the word "dhamma" does not include all phenomena such as visible forms; rather, it is said, "Mind is the forerunner of all states (dhammā)," in order to show the intended phenomenon.

The impact upon visible forms and so on means the meeting of those consciousnesses with the visible forms; since this is appropriate to say, it is stated as "the mere impact (abhinipāta) of visible forms and so on." Alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative (kamma). This is because visible forms and so on are what should be impacted by the consciousnesses. The intended meaning in the passages beginning with "This is what is meant" is as follows: excluding visible forms and so on which should be known by making them objects, these five consciousnesses do not have the cognition of wholesome and unwholesome volition, the states associated with that volition, and the states such as adverting which are the forerunners of the aforementioned five consciousnesses and which should be known by them. By doing so, he prohibits functions other than seeing and so on, stating, "These five consciousnesses do not have what is called specific cognition (paṭiviññatti) of wholesome states and so on, which is distinct from the mere function of seeing (dassana) and so on."

Because of the state of being non-resultant (avipāka), he includes wholesome and unwholesome states without excluding other general indeterminate (abyākata) states. He also prohibits the function ending with death (cuti). By the word "pi," process-consciousnesses (vīthicitta) together with javana are combined, and the intention in prohibiting them at the five doors would be: "If with a corrupted mind... with a confident mind, one speaks or acts"—only those powerful states occurring at the sixth door (mind-door) which perform speaking and acting as preached, and those similar states which produce happiness and suffering, are taken by the word "dhamma." Therefore, there is no cognition of those states by the javana occurring at the five doors. However, cognition by way of being a forerunner of the weak five-door processes is not prohibited therein.
201:
"Does not initiate bodily action, nor initiate vocal action" is understood because of the permission of weak mental action, by negating the initiation of only the production of consciousness that causes the two types of intimation (viññatti). Likewise, the undertaking of wholesome or unwholesome states, such as "I will perform wholesome bodily conduct," or its opposite, "I will perform unwholesome action," does not occur by means of javana at the five doors. Similarly, in the explanation of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), it is said: "Death (cuti) at the five doors also does not occur by five-door consciousnesses, because the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) does not occur in those doors." This is the meaning.

There is the Pali: "By the five consciousnesses, one does not cognize any phenomenon (dhamma) other than the mere impact (abhinipāta)." In that Pali, the meaning is clear: excluding the mere impact of visible forms and so on, one cannot cognize any other nature of phenomena. This is because even though eye-consciousness receives a visible form, it cannot grasp it as "a visible form." Since the receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana) also does not have the cognition of aspects such as the blue color of the visible form, the cognition of any phenomenon is negated. However, because there is an excellent cognition of that object by the five consciousnesses, it is not said (of sampaṭicchana, etc.) that it is "other than the mere impact." For those who desire the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā) other than that for which the Pali states the nature of having external and present objects, the co-arising of the analytical knowledge with five-door javana is prohibited. "Rūpārūpadhamme" means the states of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara).

Why is it said, "One does not wake up by five-door consciousness"? Is it not that when visible forms and so on come into the focus (āpātha), one wakes up from sleep? No, it is not so. To show that the mind-door javana arises first, he said "niddāyantassa hi," etc. Some teachers say it is only indeterminate (abyākata) because, being enticed by a true dream, mere adverting arises. It should be understood that those teachers intend that even in the mind-door, adverting arises two or three times, stands in the place of javana, and then subsides into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

"Tassā eva vasena" means that by the power of that wisdom alone, it is the locus of knowledge in another way; the words should be construed as "it should be known."

## The Explanation of the Description of the Ones is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Description of the Twos

With the intention that the word "attha," when taking the sense of nature (sabhāva) in other contexts and occurring in locative cases, undergoes a change of gender (liṅga) by the power of the locative...
202:
It should be understood that the meaning 'jāpitattha' (accomplished benefit) has been clearly explained because it is the benefit that has been brought about.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Dyads is finished.

## 3. The Explanation of the Exposition of the Triads

'Paññā-pariṇāmitesu' means [in spheres of work, etc.] that have been ripened (brought to completion) by wisdom. The term 'yoga-vihitesu' (arranged by application) is merely a specification of the object where wisdom is established. Therefore, all past, present, and future spheres of work, etc., that are arranged by wisdom should be understood as 'yoga-vihita'. An art that must be learned and then performed is called 'sippa' (craft), while other work [performed without learning] is called 'kamma' (action). This is the distinction between the two. In the term 'vaḍḍhakī-kamma' (carpentry), the coarse work that can be done without learning should be understood as 'kamma'. Alternatively, wisdom itself in those various instances should be known as 'kamma' or 'sippa'. What is called 'nāga-maṇḍala' is the art of removing poison by forming a circle, summoning snakes with mantras, and giving offerings. 'Paritta' (protection) is the art of guarding against danger, and by that art, people remove poison by blowing with the mouth, saying 'phū'. The mantra for curing [bites from] spiders and such is called 'phu-dhamanaka-mantra'. The brief matrices starting with 'A, Ā' and the various detailed forms starting with 'Ka, Kā' are called 'lekhā' (the art of writing).

Wholesome states are 'one's own property' (because they bring welfare and happiness). Other unwholesome states are 'not one's own property' (because they bring harm and suffering). The four truths that are to be penetrated should be understood as 'anulomana' (conformity) by way of being the cause for such penetration. Previously, wisdom was spoken of by terms such as 'yoga-vihitesu vā kamma-yatanesu', and again, it was spoken of as 'anulomika-khanti' (conformity-patience), etc., by way of synonyms for that wisdom; with this intention, it was said, 'anulomika... etc., are synonyms for wisdom'. Here, 'evarūpiṃ' (of such a nature) means having the objects such as the aforementioned spheres of work, having the nature of conformity to the truth of ownership of deeds (kammassakatā), and having the mode of occurrence such as impermanence. The aforementioned descriptions of the planes, natures, and modes of occurrence should be connected with patience (khanti), etc. That wisdom which can endure the reflection—defined as the function of absolute scrutiny and specific knowing of states (such as spheres of work)—because it has an undistorted nature, is called 'dhamma-nijjhānakkhanti' (patience in reflecting on the Dhamma), meaning that in that wisdom, there is the capacity to endure the reflection on states.

Because it abandons non-restraint (asaṃvara), the volition associated with the abstinence of undertaking (samādāna-virati) and the abstinence of encountering (sampatta-virati) is called 'the volition of release (muñca-cetanā) of one fulfilling virtue'. Since the nature of being consisting in giving and virtue of the wisdom occurring in the preceding and succeeding moments has been stated, it is appropriate to say 'ārabbha' (beginning) by way of the volition of release and the subsequent volition, and 'adhikicca' (concerning) by way of the preceding volition; thus, the reading 'adhikiccā' is also suitable.
203:
The five precepts and the ten precepts are included in the formations and existences (saṅkhāra-bhava) which are the causes of consciousness and birth; they have been included in the Dhamma-ṭṭhiti text beginning with 'Uppādā vā' (Whether [Tathāgatas] arise). The prescription of virtue that brings about [favorable] existence, even if it is heard [from the Buddha], is not dependent solely on the Buddha's teaching (as it can also occur outside the dispensation); thus, this prescription of virtue was spoken of for bhikkhus and others.

Wisdom included within higher wisdom (adhipaññā) is called 'wisdom belonging to higher wisdom'. Alternatively, the term 'adhipaññā' should be understood as referring to the states (Path and Fruit) produced by higher wisdom, or the states (insight) that are the basis for that higher wisdom; the wisdom occurring in those states is called 'wisdom belonging to higher wisdom'.

Thinking whether skill in bringing about ruin could be 'apāya-kosalla' (skill in loss), one asks: 'How can skill in loss be called wisdom?' To refute that person's intention, [the Buddha] said: 'Only one who has wisdom...', etc. 'Tatrūpāyā' means the means (wisdom) in those various matters. The arising [of that knowledge] at the occasion of its occurrence is called 'ṭhānuppatti' (presence of mind). What is that knowledge? It is the knowing of the cause; it means arising quickly at that very place (at that very moment) when danger, etc., arise.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Triads is finished.

## 4. The Explanation of the Exposition of the Tetrads

'He does not yearn or tremble' (na paritassati) means he does not yearn, thinking 'It would be good if I had provisions such as rice,' or he does not tremble because of the absence of those provisions.

'Not dependent on others' (aparappaccaya) means not being made to believe by others. 'Knowledge of the Dhamma' (dhamme ñāṇaṃ) means knowledge having the four truths as its object. Indeed, the noble truths are called 'Dhamma' because they have an undistorted nature. Alternatively, the Noble Path, which is the best among conditioned things, and its fruit are called 'Dhamma'; the wisdom associated with that Path and Fruit is 'knowledge of the Dhamma'. It is not the producing of another knowledge or the leading of a method, but rather it is the function of reviewing knowledge; with this intention, it is said: 'the function of reviewing knowledge'. Here, 'by this Dhamma' (iminā dhammena) means by the knowledge of the Path; however, since both the knowledge of the Path and the Fruit are the basis for reviewing and the cause for leading the method, it is not inappropriate to say 'by those two dhammas'. Likewise, because the Dhamma of the four truths has been known, and because the Dhamma called Path and Fruit has reached association with right view that penetrates the truths, it is the leading of the method; therefore, this...
204:
The meaning "by the Dhamma known either as an object of knowledge or by association with knowledge" is also not inappropriate (it is indeed appropriate). Although they know suffering in all its aspects—past, future, and present—because there is a particular firm application of mind to the present suffering included within one's own continuity, it is said: "not only that (past and future), but also this (present)." It is called Nayana-ñāṇa (or Naya-ñāṇa) because of the inference regarding the unseen Truth through the seen Truth. It is called Kāraṇa-ñāṇa because it is the cause for seeing the unseen Truth. Alternatively, since the word kāraṇa expresses a suitable meaning, it means knowledge conformable to the knowledge of the Dhamma (Anurūpa-ñāṇa).

Conventional knowledge (Sammuti-ñāṇa) refers to knowledge included among those things designated as knowledge by the mere generality of knowing that illuminates the object, without the extraordinary function of penetration like the knowledge of the Dhamma and others. Alternatively, it is called Sammuti-ñāṇa because it occurs by way of convention. The remaining knowledge, being dissimilar to the other three types of knowledge, is to be understood as Sammuti-ñāṇa because it is included in conventional knowledge by that very generality of dissimilarity.

"Kilesamūlaka" refers to the states of sensual existence rooted in the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).

In the phrase "sā hissa", "assa" refers to that person endowed with the first absorption (paṭhamajjhāna) who is described as "one who is dispassionate towards sensual pleasures." By the word "sveva", while taking the person endowed with the first absorption at the moment of developing dispassion towards sensual pleasures, it is said "being one who is dispassionate towards sensual pleasures" to show the subsequent state of that person after that first absorption. The wisdom of the fourth path is said to penetrate the sixth supernormal power because it attains the state of the sixth supernormal power (āsavakkhaya). Other path-wisdoms are said to penetrate it because they are the strong dependence for that supernormal power. Alternatively, the wisdom in all four paths should be understood as penetrating the sixth supernormal power because of the destruction of taints (āsava) as appropriate, or because of producing that fruit when the destruction of taints, which is the fruit, occurs.

"Kāmasahagata" means having the object of physical sensuality (vatthukāma). "Codenti" means they urge towards sensual pleasures, making the mind incline towards them. "Tadanudhammatā" means simply "tadanudhamma". Since the suffix "tā" has no additional special meaning, it is said "having such a conformable nature." Attachment (nikanti), or the arising of consciousness associated with attachment, is called "wrong mindfulness" (micchāsati). The perceptions and mental applications that take the absorption without initial application as an object, thinking "O, would that the absorption without initial application might arise in me!", are called "accompanied by the absence of initial application" (avitakkasahagata).
205:
It means one who knows directly (abhijānanta) by way of attainment, or one who knows with distinguished knowledge, making manifest that state of the path which is not an object of the absorptions.

An absorption devoid of the five masteries (vasībhāva) is called "unskilled" (appaguṇa). In this Catukka-niddesa, by pointing out the modes of progress and objects of wisdom through the four modes of progress and four objects, wisdom itself is pointed out, and that very wisdom is analyzed in detail.

## The Explanation of the Fourfold Section is finished.

## 5. The Explanation of the Fivefold Section

By the words "fivefold Right Concentration", wisdom is presented as a factor of concentration. Through words such as "pervading with rapture" (pīti-pharaṇatā), that very wisdom is analyzed in detail. The pervading of rapture and happiness should be understood by the method: "That person pervades this very body with rapture and happiness born of seclusion," and so on. Because of establishing the fourth absorption by standing on the object through the pervading of rapture and the pervading of happiness, those wisdoms are said to be "like feet."

In the second fivefold section, by the Pali "concentration with fivefold knowledge", the five knowledges themselves are shown briefly and in detail, with concentration as the heading. The adversaries of mundane concentration, such as the hindrances and attachment to the first absorption, should be suppressed. Other defilements should be restrained. In this concentration of the fruit of Arahantship, however, since all defilements have been subsided, there are no defilements to be suppressed or restrained. Furthermore, it is called "concentration not reached by effort, suppression, or restraint" (na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato) because it is attained and established without volitional effort at the moment of attainment immediately following the path, or because it is established without decline. By the phrase "due to the state of having reached abundance of mindfulness," it is shown that even when mindfulness is not currently occurring, one is called "mindful" due to the abundance of mindfulness. By the phrase "by way of the delimited time," it is shown that one is called "mindful" by the mindfulness that delimits the time.

## The Explanation of the Fivefold Section is finished.
206:
## 6. Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā
Desiring to show the manifestation of the state of purity, he said: "dūra...pe... rammanāya." By the term "sotadhātuvisuddhi" (purity of the ear-element), the mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) included in the ear-element are taught; therefore, the knowledge (ñāṇa) that is present as the chief among those states is called the knowledge in the purity of the ear-element. It should be understood that this very "cetopariyañāṇa" (knowledge of the penetration of others' minds) is extracted as "paracitte ñāṇa" (knowledge regarding others' minds) according to its meaning. Because the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (cutūpapātañāṇa) is a part of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), it is spoken of as "vaṇṇadhātu-ārammaṇa" (having the element of color/form as its object). It should be understood that by the divine eye knowledge, which is the knowledge of passing away and rebirth that has reached its peak, the whole is called "dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa."

## Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 7. Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā
In the phrase "tadeva ñāṇaṃ," the meaning is that the sixfold knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) is taken together with its status as an object of insight (vipassanā). "Dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇena" means by the knowledge that summarizes the six kinds of knowledge. Indeed, showing the knowledge that occurs in various ways such as "khayadhamma" (subject to destruction) is merely insight into insight (vipassanā-paṭivipassanā), because it shows how to practice insight on preceding knowledges; therefore, the meaning is that that knowledge is not a separate factor (aṅga). However, since the factors are taught everywhere in the Pāḷi text by the word "ñāṇa," the meaning is clear that only the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) revealed by the word "iti" as "nirodhadhammanti ñāṇaṃ" is the seventh knowledge. Indeed, it is not possible to connect it as "that dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa is also a single knowledge," because in taking that word "ñāṇa," there is no intention to show the state of knowledge in this dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa, and because it would lead to having no word to connect with "khayadhamma...pe... nirodhadhamma."

## Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 8. Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā
"Vihāritabbaṭṭhena" is because of the meaning of having cut off opposing states or, alternatively, suffering (dukkha).

## Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.
